speechtext: Hon. Arthur Meighen (Minister of the Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 168 to amend the Irrigation Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This Bill provides for expropriation, where necessary, of inferior water rights for the benefit of superior water rights. In the original Act domestic, municipal, commercial, and irrigation water rights are given orders of preference in the order named. It has been found that in practice where the first or second or third, as the case may be, develops to be more essential than the second, third or fourth, there must be power to expropriate the inferior rights, paying for them what may be necessary, in order that the higher and more essential rights may not suffer. That is the main object of the Bill. One other purpose is to provide that water derivable from springs shall be in the same position as to federal control as other waters.

speechtext: On Tuesday last my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries promised to give some information on the following day as to the delays which have occurred in the sailing of the steamship " Canadian Inventor" owing to some trouble between the company and its employees. Can the minister give us the information today?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. C. BALLANTYNE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: SS. CANADIAN INVENTOR - DELAYED IN SAILING.
speechtext: I would have given the information yesterday but that my hon. friend did not happen to be in his seat when the Orders of the Day were called. As I stated the other day, one of the causes of the delay was a strike of the painters. Happily, that has now been settled. I have also ascertained that the Coughlan Shipbuilding Company did not make the ship's shaft according to specifications, and therefore the inspection by Lloyd's and by one of our inspectors of the Marine Department has been withheld until the shafting has been adjusted. I understand this also has been attended to. The vessel is now in dry dock, owing to her having been in the water since January last. One of the clauses in the specifications provides for the docking of the vessel if the Marine Department finds that is necessary. I do not anticipate that there is anything wrong with the bottom of the ship, but inasmuch as she has to make a very long trip to Australia it was thought wise to have her docked. As far as I can judge at the moment, she ought to be ready to sail within two weeks, and probably less.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: House again in committee on Bill No. 153 (from the Senate), (from 7th June), respecting the Director of Coal Operations, Mr. Steele in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When this Bill was
last before the committee section 1 had been considered and adopted. Section 2 is now under consideration; shall the section carry?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this Bill was before the committee at a former sitting I took strong exception to the minister asking Parliament to ratify and confirm matters of which the members of this House have no knowledge, and have had no opportunity of considering. This section is as fallows:
The orders heretofore issued by the Director of Coal Operations set forth in the schedule hereto attached are hereby ratified and confirmed and shall be deemed to have been lawfully made on the respective dates when they were signed by the said Director of Coal Operations.
Then there follows in the schedule not the text but the numbers of orders numbering from 1 to 144. Several of these orders are alphabetically subdivided, so that in fact there is a total of about 170 orders. The Bill was held over, that the House might have opportunity to see the orders, and I have in my hand the volume of orders which were issued by the Director

of Coal Operations. It is a volume very much larger tHan any compilation of statutes which might be made. as a result of the labours of four or five sessions of Parliament. I have gone through the orders in a hurried way and I find that they relate to all manner of subjects, the fixing of the rates of wages to be paid in different mines, the prices at which coal is to be mined, and the classes of labour to be employed; in a broad way they resemble the kind of legislation one finds in the reign oif Queen Elizabeth, when the State undertook to regulate matters relating to wages and prices in accordance with the spirit of that age. I shall not take up the time of the House more than to illustrate the danger there is in Parliament attempting to ratify and confirm these orders, and to give them the force of legal enactment; I shall quote one or two sections of one order to show hon. members the kind of thing they will be enacting if they pass this clause. Order 141 contains the following:
All men who work in and around the mines who are eligible to become members of the United Mine Workers of America must join that organization and agree to sign check-off for all dues, assessments and fines, and the management of the mines agree to forward deductions made to the Acting Secretary of the District or such other persons as that official may designate.
The foregoing clause to become effective vhenever the officials of the United Mine Workers of America appear on the ground in each locality and co-operate with the operators in arranging details.
It is agreed that no man will be employed or be permitted to remain in the employ of the company unless he agrees to comply with the foregoing conditions.
If we enact into law these various orders it means amongst other things that this Parliament is providing that in these mines in the West no workers can be employed unless they belong to the United Mine Workers of America. That may or may not be advisable-I am not raising that question one way or the other-I should however, like Parliament to understand what it is doing, should it blindly endorse and ratify and thereby transform into permanent legislation orders issued to deal with a particular situation. I think this one clause is quite sufficient to illustrate the danger of enacting into law a great mass of regulations and orders which no member of this House has seen. If the Director of Coal Operations has been acting within the scope of his authority in issuing these orders no exception can be taken to them. If, as stated by the minister in introducing the

Bill, the parties are agreed in reference to these orders, why not leave [DOT]them in agreement and allow that mutual understanding to decide matters? To give legislative force and sanction to these orders is simply to introduce into this country a system of compulsory arbitration which thus far we have not felt justified in instituting in Canada. These orders will have all the force of a statute once Parliament confirms and ratifies them; the parties to them will become liable to penalties at law, and the labour of the country will be brought into the position occupied by labour in countries where compulsory enactments govern the relations between employers and employees. I do not think that such a departure is wise; I believe it is departing from sound principle and, I hope the minister will not find it necessary to press this particular clause.
There is one other feature which might be considered and that is, whether or not this Parliament has the right to legislate in matters of contract such as wages and prices and other questions arising between employer and employee, and whether such matters do not properly come within the scope of provincial rather than of federal jurisdiction. There is at least, a doubt in the matter, and I think that where a doubt exists, the objections being as strong as they are to this kind of wholesale legislation, the Government would be well advised to let the Bill rest with confirming the Orders in Council giving power to the Director of Coal Operations to do what he has hitherto done, and not attempt to give legislative force to all of the orders he has issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If there is anything in the principle which the hon. member urges, it would be just as effective against the portion of the Bill which he purposes to allow to pass as against the portion he opposes. If the Orders in Council are confirmed, then undoubtedly legislation is passed of the character to which he objects. The only effect of the last clause is to still any possibility of litigation as to the effectiveness of the various orders of the Coal Director, which were based on the Orders in Council. It simply obviates the possibility of dispute, and that is all. Certainly, if the Orders in. Council are ratified, then a measure of compulsory arbitration, under the circumstances that existed when the orders were passed and that still exist, is ratified. Unquestionably there was a measure of compulsory arbitration; unquestionably it was essential; and just as unquestionably
it was called for by both parties to the dispute. There was no other way of getting the coal. What is the use in one breath of crying to the Government to see that coal is mined, and then in the next breath saying to the Government: " Don't do anything yourselves to get the coal mined "? This is the step that was taken. It proved effective and is proving effective to-day. Why therefore upset it? We are only asking that the course that has been pursued at the request of both parties be legalized in order that all parties, not merely through their representatives but individually on both sides, may be bound by it. That is essential. All we are asking is that what has proved a successful means of getting coal be ratified by this House until next session. If Parliament next session chooses in any way to modify them Parliament is free to do so and if Parliament does nothing, then the whole legislation dies at the close of the session. The order which the hon. gentleman read does .apparently just what he says. It provides that employees shall be members of the United Mine Workers of America. There may be some objection in principle to that-I do not know; but I do know that had it not been for these very orders we would not have had any coal mined. It may have been that there was lacking reason .and moderation on one side or the other; doubtless it was lacking on both sides, but we did the very best we could and got the best man we could get to go out there and see what was the best thing to be done. He went out there, did his best and succeeded. We do not want any litigation to arise over what has been done. We do not want any difficulty to be created by isolated, discontented parties, perhaps when the public interest is best served as well as the general interest of all the parties to the dispute.

This is the most amazing Bill that has ever been submitted to this Parliament in my memory. The whole Bill . is bad. If the hon. the Minister of the Interior desires to confer certain powers upon this coal commissioner, he should come forward with distinct authority by statute to confer these powers. Irrespective of any Order in Council, he should bring in a Bill in the same way as he does in any other case. We are legislating here and legislating in a most marvellous way. We are supposed to have certain well defined procedure to guard against hasty legislation. In certain cases you must first bring forward a resolution, it must stand on the

Order Paper for a while, and then you must discuss it in Committee of the Whole. Then you must proceed to get a Bill and that Bill must go through its first reading, it must go through its-second reading and it must go through its third reading. All these are parts of the machinery devised to enable an intelligent Parliament to deal intelligently with important questions. Every one of these principles is disregarded when we are asked to declare hy Act of Parliament that 144 regulations, not one of which has ever been read in this House, are legal and -are declared to be legal. It is the mo-st amazing proposition that was ever made. I cannot imagine the Government are serious in asking us to do such a thing. We have been asked to do a good many things and to confirm a good many acts which have lacked authority, but this is the worst of all. The only section of these regulations that we know anything about is the one section which has been read by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, dealing with the delicate question of the relations between capital and labour, and declaring for a principle which may be good or bad, but one that this legislature has never hitherto declared for-that a man shall not be permitted to work anywhere unless he joins a particular trades union. That is a fair question for the labouring men themselves, but we have never before been asked to declare in this House that a man must be obliged to join a trades union in order to be permitted to work. We have no knowledge of this extraordinary budget of laws except the sentence that the leader of the Opposition has quoted. It is too difficult to argue. The idea that this House shall be deliberately asked to pass these laws, not one of which has ever been submitted to the House, and not one of which hon. members know a single thing about, is so extraordinary that one cannot understand how it ever came to be suggested. I do not hesitate to say that this is the most amazing proposition that has ever been made to the Parliament of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would like to tell my hon. friend that he was for many years a member of a Government that did in effect precisely what we propose now. This is not the first time that this course has been pursued. The same course was taken by his Minister of the Interior on more than one occasion. I myself, some fourteen or fifteen years -ago, induced the

then Minister of the Interior to provide that the very numerous regulations which were enacted by his department under authority of law should be laid upon the table of this House and of the Senate within a certain period after the commencement of the session and that they should have force and effect until the end of the session and no longer unless by resolution of both Houses of Parliament they were affirmed and approved. I venture to say that on more than one occasion a budget of regulations was brought down by the then Minister of the Interior which was quite as lengthy as that which has been laid on the table of the House by the present Minister of the Interior. I recollect very well that I had, when leader of the Opposition, to detail a strong committee of my side of the House and that they had to devote their attention for a week or ten days at a time in order to gather some idea of the substance of the scores of regulations that were brought down. My hon. friend thought it was all right then. What is the difference between what he then supported and what he now condemns? According to my humble comprehension, there is absolutely no difference whatever. There is a certain responsibility cast upon the ministers of the Crown in connection with this matter as well as a responsibility cast upon Parliament and I desire to emphasize what has already been said by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, that if it had not been for these Orders in Council, passed under the War Measures Act, and if it had not been for the unremitting attention and devotion of the Director of Coal Operations, if it had not been for the most anxious consideration day and night given by the Government to his representations when matters were in a most critical state, there would have been intense suffering inflicted upon a very large proportion of the population of this country. It was only by a very narrow margin on many occasions that we succeeded in preventing such conditions in the operation of these coal mines as would have inflicted that suffering. Now the Minister of the Interior, after these regulations have been acted upon for years, simply desires that any doubt shall be removed as to their validity and that no one shall have [DOT] any ground for technical objection or obstruction in a court of law. They are not new orders; they are orders which have been acted upon and which have been put to the test of experience.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), has but one purpose and that purpose he has communicated to the House-the purpose of preventing any trivial or technical objection being raised to the operation or validity of these orders.

I do not wish to discuss the merits of the actions of the Controller of Coal. It may be that what my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) says is correct, that what was done had a very beneficial effect. I have not raised that question at all. If all that my right hon. friend says be true, and although he may prove that I have been somewhat inconsistent-suppose that may be admitted for the moment, although I do not admit it-does that alter the merits of the question, does it affect the question of the responsibility of other hon. members of this House? They are not responsible for what I did years ago if I did what the right hon. gentleman says. I have no recollection of the particular orders to which my right hon. friend refers, but according to his own statement these orders proposed to make certain regulations and they were submitted to this House for the approval of Parliament. It was not a case where we were not submitting them to the House for approval. But here is a case where regulations have been passed for months and things have been done under them, some of which may not have been legal, and we are asked now to declare that everything that was done under these regulations was legal. The right hon. gentle-, man says that their object in proposing this legislation is to prevent any question arising hereafter. If they acted lawfully why do they want a whitewashing Act of this kind? If they acted unlawfully, why do they want a whitewashing Act?
If it is lawful then they do not need this thing. I again say to my hon. friend that I have no recollection of the cases mentioned by the Minister of the Interior. I assume that what my hon. friend says in that respect is correct, although I think even as he states it the minister brought down, under authority, a body of regulations which were to be approved if they remained on the table of the House for a given period and were not condemned. However, I do not want to dwell on that. The hon. member may perhaps be right, if it serves any good purpose in saying that I am inconsistent, although I do not think I am. However, that is not the point to-day. The point is, that this Parliament ought not to be
called upon, not only to authorize these things in the future, tout to authorize those things that have been done in the past when they may not be legal. Are we going to set aside all thought of legislative power by this Parliament and allow the Government to lead us blindly not only in endorsing everything as to matters about which we are informed, but also as to things that we do not know anything about?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In reply to
my hon. friend I have to say that the distinction which he has attempted to draw does not exist. The Orders in Council to which I have alluded were not passed by the Minister of the Interior but by the Governor in Council upon his recommendation, and after having been so passed they came into immediate operation and continued in operation until the end of the following session of Parliament, but no longer unless they were approved. I do not think that very much fault can be found with such a practice because the regulations are of so minute a character , and so exceedingly numerous, that it would have been utterly impossible for Parliament to occupy its time properly in dealing with administrative orders of that character; it would be utterly impossible for Parliament to undertake administration in that way. But inasmuch as important matters of administration might be involved, inasmuch as matters of policy in some cases might be involved, I persuaded the Minister of the Interior of that day to depart from the practice which had prevailed before and to have these Orders in Council operate only until end of next session of Parliament, unless ratified in the meantime by resolution of the House. But what is this situation? Precisely the same. The Government had power under the War Measures Act to make certain Orders in Council. Under these Orders in Council a Director of Coal Operations was appointed. He has done his work and I think he has done it well. I think his work has prevented a great deal of suffering which otherwise might have been inflicted upon the people of this country. The War Measures Act is no longer to be acted upon. Therefore we come to Parliament asking it, from the very necessity of the situation, to continue these Orders in Council until the end of the next session, and no longer, just as the regulations of the Minister of the Interior in the old days were continued until the end of the next following session and no longer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And the game
practice prevails now in the legislation of the Minister of the Interior. Therefore I hope my hon. friend will not think that under the circumstances there is any divergence in this respect from the practice that has been pursued in the past. I alluded to the action of the old Government merely for the purpose of showing the established practice in respect of administrative orders which had to be brought to the consideration of Parliament but which could not be enacted, or dealt with in the first instance by Parliament itself. What was the practice in those days continues to be the practice still in the Department of the Interior; and in dealing with this matter as we did under the War Measures Act, and in bringing the matter to the attention of Parliament as the Minister of the Interior has brought it .today, we are simply carrying out a principle embodied in that practice and acted upon not only by this Government but by the Government which preceded it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend has spoken of the Orders in Council that were passed conferring authority upon the Director of Coal Operations and from his remarks I would judge he feels that we are proposing in some way to take away the power that has been given the Director of Coal Operations under these Orders in Council. We have no intention of doing that. As a matter of fact the powers, duties and rights given to the Director of Coal Operations under Orders in Council are expressly continued. Now we are going a long way, I think, in ratifying those Orders in Council, and continuing them for another year. If we had taken exception to giving these powers under Order in Council, and had required them to be expressed in legislation through a Bill brought into the House and discussed in all its stages, we would have perhaps been taking a course more consistent with the protection of public rights in the matter. What we are taking exception to now is that having granted certain rights to the Director of Coal Operations by Order in Council, we are being asked by section 2 to confirm as legal everything that that Director of Coal Operations has done, whether or not he has gone beyond the powers given him by Order in Council. If the Director of Coal Operations has not exceeded any powers given him by Order in Council then all these orders which have been issued by him will be perfectly valid. But if he has exceeded those powers and has gone further than he was authorized to do

by Order in Council, why should not the parties who may be aggrieved have the right of redress? This measure proposes to deprive of redress any man who believes that his rights have been infringed by virtue of the Director of Coal Operations having exceeded his power.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend perhaps does not quite realize the extraordinary ingenuity, on some occasions, of members of my own profession in taking exception on very technical grounds to Orders in Council -or to Statutes for that matter-even if great care has been taken in framing them. These orders have been acted upon for years, and the only purpose of the Minister of the Interior, as expressed by him, is to prevent the possibility of unnecessary and vexatious litigation, upon some minor technical point, whenever some ingenious member of the legal profession would see fit to question the exact validity and the conformity of any one of these orders of the Director of Coal Operations. The Director of Coal Operations is not a lawyer himself; he is a business man. He has had to make these orders offhand, and to couch them in his own language, and I think it would not be conducive to the public interest that minor technical objections should be raised to them on some occasion by any lawyer with an exceedingly acute mind. As I understand it that is all my hon. friend, the Minister of the Interior, has in mind.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If my right
hon. friend's remarks mean anything they *nean that the person who has been appointed to this office is a man who may or may not make blunders, and that if he has made blunders there is to be no mode of redress in regard to those blunders. I would ask the Minister of the Interior if any exception has been taken by any one to any order that has been issued. Has any one of them been called in question?
Sir ROBERT BO'1"'"' Before the Minister of the Interior answers the question I would ask my hon. friend whether he knows of any human being in his acquaintance who is not liable to make blunders some time?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I would answer my right hon. friend by saying that I do not, but inasmuch as human nature is apt to err it is necessary to take precautions to see that when that does occur the rights of third parties shall not be prejudiced thereby. We believe that the Director of Coal Operations, being human, may

have exceeded hie powers in a manner which may have injured third parties, and we on this side are asking that Parliament should not take from any person who has been deprived of his rights the recourse to that redress which the law of the land affords. I am quite prepared to admit with my right hon. friend that lawyers may be fond of technicalities-
Question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: -but the law means something and justice means something, and we have the law to see that justice is done. I do not think we should take away from individuals who are not lawyers the right of getting redress to /which under the principles of ordinary justice they are entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have no difficulty at all in answering the hon. member. The Director o-f Coal Operations has been discharging hi6 duties for, I think, three or four years. At 'the present time I am not aware of one single objection on legal grounds to anything he has done; so far as I know the Minister of Labour has never been informed of any; certainly there is no substantial matter in dispute. Undoubtedly all the director's decisions were questioned on grounds of policy and of fairness by both sides, but they were acquiesced in generally. Now, is it going to be a matter of justice or injustice to pass this legislation? Suppose the ingenuity of the legal profession can find that some excess of power was exercised and acquiesced in under an order made, say, three years ago and acted on ever since; is there going to be more suffering and injustice by upsetting 'the whole thing and injuring rights that accrued by virtue of the order,-unscrambling the whole state of affairs, than by quieting and settling matters as acquiesced in by both sides? Which course is going to most conduce to order and justice? If a person can find something technically wrong with any of these orders, that person may not have suffered at all, the defect may be something really trivial and technical in character; but if he upsets the order, who else is going to suffer but innocent parties everywhere? And there will be confusion in control, and parties who ought not to suffer at all are sure to suffer. In a word, there will be a thousand times more suffering by upsetting any of these orders than could possibly follow by Parliament quieting and settling matters as they are at present. I admit that if some substantial question of law were in dispute between the parties it would not ordinarily be right for Parliament to come in and get on the side of either party in an endeavour to settle the dispute. But that is not the case here at all; there is no question in dispute that I know of. I do not know whether there is likely to be any dispute, but clearly as both sides have acquiesced in everything to date, if there be any dispute it must be purely technical or we would have heard of it.
And look at what would happen if that question when raised should be upheld by the courts. That is the reason for our taking this course. It is not that we are getting on the side of any litigant, it is not that we are seeking to do injustice; we are seeking to stop a process that might lead to great injustice.

I am sorry that the hon. the Minister of Finance is not present as he might gather from the observations of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of the Interior that he would have an opportunity to save a great deal of money if he could just simply abolish the courts, because that is what is proposed to be done here. Both the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior have spoken of the ingenuity of the legal profession. Do they imagine that that ingenuity is likely to be confined to seeking flaws in legislation of this character? Do they not know that that ingenuity can be applied to question-' ing every Act we pass here? I venture to say that for a $500 fee you can engage an able lawyer to raise doubts as to the propriety of any Act of Parliament. But we do not consider that a sufficient reason for validating everything that has been done. The Minister of the Interior says that so far as he knows there is no question in dispute between the parties. If 'that is so, what is the necessity for this legislation? And if there is any question in dispute, why should we undertake to turn out of court any man in this Dominion who has or imagines he has a grievance? You can dismiss any man's case by saying it is of a trivial or a technical character; but no point of law is trivial or technical to the man whose honour, person or property is affected. And I say that all the arguments advanced 'by the Prime Minister regarding the ingenuity of the legal profession furnish no sufficient reason why we should turn out of court any man whose interests may be affected by these orders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think what is proposed by the Minister of the Interior is
3:366

very mild indeed compared with some legislation to which my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) committed himself in days gone hy, because I can recollect that he caused to be passed by the Legislature of Nova Scotia an Act taking away the right of action from individuals. Surely this is a very mild dose of Parliamentary ratification compared with that Act.

My right hon. friend shows the weakness of his case when he undertakes to refer to some alleged legislation which I was connected with in times past. I do not know to what the right hon. gentleman refers, and I do not think he has good ground for what he states. But surely to argue that because I did a wrong some years ago is good reason for the action of the Government in this instance, shows the inherent weakness of the position now taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The member for Shelburne and Queen's rose in his place and pronounced this legislation the most amazing in character and principle that he had ever heard of.
I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Then it is not at all
relevant to show that he was himself a party to like legislation on other occasions?
No.

Two blacks do not
make a white.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
But is this the most
amazing legislation if he himself has put through legislation of the same character? If he had not himself made the comparison, perhaps he might shield himself behind the fact that two wrongs do not make a right. But he stated to the House that there had never been anything like this since the days of Confederation. We have shown that he is wrong.
No, you have not.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We can show the same thing on the pages of every statute since Confederation.
All right; show it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Only last year what
was done when the Newsprint Control was continued? Why did not my hon. friend pronounce that to be an amazing innovation? Newsprint Controller, first of all stalled by Order in Council under the War Measures Act, was confirmed in office, his actions were approved, and litigation was

stopped. The regulations that the Prime Minister refers to were brought into this House and had to be approved by this Parliament. Never have they been written out in the law, they have always been laid on the table of the House, and therefore one might say that they have been approved in the aggregate. Would any one suggest that we ought to embody that whole volume of Orders in Council in a statute?
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no other way of doing it than the way we are following now. It is the proper thing to do, and certainly will conduce to less injustice than any other course we might take.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have ventured to cite only one of these orders, but I think perhaps it would be well to give the House some further information as to the nature of others. If the minister looks at regulation 124 he will find it provides that nine hours' pay shall be given for eight hours' work. I want to ask my hon. friends opposite:	Is that a
principle that we as a Parliament wish to endorse? If it is to be adopted for the miners in British Columbia, why should it not be adopted also for the miners in other provinces? Why should we legislate to give nine hours' pay for eight hours' work to one body of men who happen to belong to one particular trade union, and at the same time enact that no man shall get the benefit of that increased pay unless he belongs to that particular union? It is not consonant with the defence of individual rights and liberties for Parliament to enact such legislation. Then take order 136, which gives boys over eighteen years of age the pay of a man. If a boy of eighteen is to receive a man's pay in these particularly favoured regions, why should he not get it in other parts of the Dominion?
The real point at issue is not the particular local situation in British Columbia, because the laws of this Parliament are made for the whole Dominion; it is whether Parliament itself shall be brought into contempt by enacting a mass of legislation of which it is wholly uninformed. Here is a mass of typewritten orders of practically 1,000 pages, fixing the hours of wages, the rates to be charged for the different mining operations, the price to be paid for coal, and providing for all kinds of special conditions which may or may not arise. Now, if the Director of Coal Operations has exercised his powers in an honest and

fair way, no one is going to suffer by allowing matters to stand as they are. Hon. gentlemen opposite have on previous occasions said that we should let well enough alone. When my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) tells us there is no dispute or disagreement regarding these particular regulations, I reply:	Leave well enough alone, but do
not ask this Parliament to enact legislation which will require nine hours' pay to be paid for eight hours' work; which will allow a. workman to work in certain mines only if he belongs to a particular union; which will fix a definite price for coal which cannot be changed either way whether the operator wishes to change it or not; which changes the rate of wages, the hours of labour, and other matters affecting the miners irrespective of whether they wish it or not. There are principles that are fundamental in this matter. It is bad enough to carry on industy in that fashion under Orders in Council, it is wholly inexcusable for Parliament to give its sanction to that kind of paternalism and favouritism.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The point raised by the hon. member is well worth a moment's discussion. Parliament, by ratifying these orders, does not support any principle such as the hon. member calls in question; it does not take any side one way or the other. In this emergent case, in order that coai might be produced and that people might live rather than freeze, it was found neces-211
sary to make orders of this character. It is in the public interest that these orders as between these parties be confirmed; that is all. Parliament takes no stand in favour of nine hours' wages for eight hours' work or for eight hours' wages for nine hours' work, nor does Parliament take a stand in favour of the closed shop or anything else of that kind. Parliament simply says that a settlement of a dispute which, had it not been settled, would have brought great hardship on the people of Western Canada, shall stand as made under the circumstances prevailing at that time. No academic question is involved; we are simply confirming settlements that have been made of disputes in a particular area for a particular purpose.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What we are doing now does not relate merely to the past. We are making these orders binding for another year, until after the next session of Parliament. When clause 1 was before the committee I suggested that instead of making these Orders in Council binding until the end of the next session we should provide for their expiration at the end of the present fiscal year. But the minister refused to do that, he was so keen on extending the period that much longer. So what we are doing now is to legislate" on these matters of wages, hours or work and prices for the period of another year.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member is not quite right. We do not fix wages or hours of work; we say that orders so made were good and that they shall stand as good. But
n	under the powers of the Orders
3 p.m. in Council which we ratify, they are alterable at any time by the man who made them. If they are found not to work well between now and the end of the next session of Parliament, they can be altered. We are simply holding the situation and determining that what has been done is legal, subject to the same powers of alteration as have all along existed.

My hon. friend says that this proposal does not support any principle one way or the other, but he will admit that if we adopt this legislation we are creating a precedent which will be relied upon in the future. For example, if the employees on the Government railways or of the Public Works Department ask for nine hours' pay for eight hours' work, the Government or Parliament cannot' very well refuse their request because they have already made a



similar arrangement with the miners in British Columbia. That is the point which I find some difficulty about. I would like the minister to explain how he is going to get rid of the precedent if Parliament adopts it in this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
' Parliament does not adapt a precedent. Parliament simply ratifies something that has been done. In itself it may have been right or it may have been wrong, but in the circumstances under which it was performed it was right and served an essential purpose. Even were a closed shop wrong, it would be far better to have a closed shop than frozen homes; we chose the one in place of the other. Now we say: do not let that be called in question; if you do there will be great confusion and great injustice. There is no precedent . about it. It may have been, as a matter of principle, right or wrong; but as a matter of emergent action it was undoubtedly right and effective.
Mr. MACKENZIE King: Does the minister see where he is getting to in the matter of future disputes? If the argument is to prevail that there must be either a closed shop or frozen homes, we may expect a good deal in the way of industrial controversy in this country that we have not hitherto experienced. Why imagine a situation when there is no ground for so doing? But my purpose in rising w.as to ask the minister if he has copies of the Orders in Council themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I will send them across to my hon. friend.

Prior to 1911, when the present leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) was Minister of Labour, he experienced great difficulties in dealing with labour troubles in that part of the country that we have been talking about,- part of Alberta and the southeasterly part of British Columbia. He did everything possible to allay the unrest that prevailed and to overcome the labour difficulties that had been experienced for some years. When we came into power in 1911 we experienced difficulties, perhaps not quite so serious as those which my hon. friend had to deal with, but difficulties just the same. Subsequently we came to the conclusion that it would be in the interests of the country to appoint a competent man to be on the ground and to give him power to deal with these difficulties as they arose. We thought then and [DOT]we think how that we found a man, in the person of the present Director

of Coal Operations, who was exceedingly well qualified to deal with such matters; a man who 'had had large experience in dealing with labour men, who had a business of his own, and who sacrificed a great deal, at our earnest solicitation, to accept this position. We could not have found in Canada a man better qualified to deal with such matters. A man of kindly disposition and conciliatory temperament, we felt sure that he	would succeed	in	getting
the employer and the employees to look at things from the same viewpoint, in the interests of the country. At that time we had authority under the War Measures Act to do certain things. To that War Measures Act Parliament agreed in August, 1914, without a dissenting voice, ilf I remember aright. It conferred certain powers upon the Governor in Council because it would have been impossible to'deal through Parliament with conditions that might arise from time to time while we were engaged in the Great War. It was under this power given to the Governor in Council that these orders were passed after August, 1914. The Coal Director was given jurisdiction over the whole province of Alberta and that portion of British Columbia from its easterly boundary to the summit of the Rocky Mountains. During the time Mr. Armstrong has been Director of Coal Operations in that vast area where there are about fifty different companies operating and producing coal, he has male all these orders. His function generally was to get the miners and their employers together and reach an agreement as to an infinite number of things-wages, hours of labour, and other conditions. The conditions differ in the fifty different companies that are operating mines in the whole province of Alberta. and the southeasterly part of British Columbia. It has been said here that 144 agreements have been entered into and sanctioned by order of the Coal Director. What happens if these orders go by the board? Some of them may extend for another year. I fancy that there are agreements entered into under orders made by Mr. Armstrong that will not terminate for another year, until the end of the next session of Parliament. You can see in a moment that if those orders are all to be done away with and we are to start in and scrutinize all these orders that have been made affecting the fifty different companies in that vast territory, we could not do it during this Parliament because we would have to hear both sides. It strikes me that it would be a very serious matter

indeed to interfere in any way with these orders that have been passed by Mr. Armstrong. It would probably bring about chaos in the mining operations in that whole area. Therefore, I regard it as of the utmost importance that sanction be given now not only to the Orders in Council touching the appointment of the Coal Director, but to the orders which he has made, the setting aside of which would bring about very serious labour troubles in that whole area.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: These Orders in Council should have been brought down along with the orders of the Director of Coal Operations. I say further, they should have been laid on the table of the House as soon as Parliament met.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
II am not sure but what they have been laid on the Table. Undoubtedly they were published in the Gazette.
(Mr. MACKENZIE KING: Now that the Orders in Council have been produced I should like to read a paragraph or two setting forth the powers given to the Director of -Coal Operations. I think Parliament will feel that with these powers about enough is being done in the way of arbitrary enactment. The Order in Council of the 25t-h of June, 1917, reads in part as follows:
2.	The Director shall have power to make all necessary investigations and inquiries respecting wages, holidays, hours of labour, and other labour conditions, and respecting all other matters necessary to, connected with or affecting the cost of and the production of coal and coke, the resumption of the production of the same, and the continuance of such production in the said district during the present war, and for three months after the end of the said war.
3.	The owner, agent and manager of every coal mine and the owner, agent and manager of every coke producing plant within the said District 18 and where the owner of any such mine or coke producing plant is a Company, every director of the Company shall comply with the orders and direction of the Director in respect of the matters specified in the last preceding paragraph and generally in connection with the management, operation and use of the mine or of the coke producing plant as the case may be and if he fails to do so he shall be guilty of a summary offence against these regulations.
Then in the Order in 'Council of the 15th of November, 1917, there is this additional power:
And whereas it is deemed expedient that the said obligations should be imposed upon the said employees, and that the Director of Coal Operations should be authorized to notify the Commissioner of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police of any failure to observe his orders and directions on the part either of said own-2141
ers, agents and managers or said employees, and that the said Commissioner should be instructed to enforce the observance of such orders and directions;
Therefore,
Certain changes are made, of which the following is the last one cited:
Upon the failure on the part of any such owner, agrent, manager or employee to comply with any of the orders and directions aforesaid the Director shall notify the Commissioner of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police of such failure, whose duty it shall then be to take such means as he may deem expedient for the enforcement of such orders and directions.
Here we have powers given by the Governor in Council to the Director of Coal Operations to do almost anything he pleases and to authorize the Northwest Mounted Police to come in and compel obedience to his orders not only by the managers, but by all the workmen in these particular mines. I think that is going about the limit by way of arbitrary enactment in dealing with industrial questions; and to come now to Parliament and say that in addition to all those powers which have already been given, and which may be exercised at any time, we should give legislative sanction to every order that has been made, whether it is in accordance with these general powers or not, is simply making Parliament a mere echo of the will of a single man who has been put in the position of an -autocrat oveT a large portion of the industrial properties of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The House at this stage may not appreciate as keenly as some of us do who were very close to the difficulty, the circumstances that obtained when these orders were passed. Undoubtedly the powers given were wide. Although I was not the minister directly in charge-indeed, I am not now the minister who is responsible initially for this Bill-still as a member of the Government I very well recall the anxious periods that we did go through just arising from and in -relation to these coal disputes in Western Canada. Tt is easy at this distance of time to look back and say that these are wide autocratic powers, and that this man was put in a position of absolute control, and surrounded with the Mounted Police to do his work. That was done, but if the hon. gentleman had had before him the perils we were faced with at that time, he would have thought it was a time for real action instead of a time for disputation and nice academic discussions about power. The steps we took had to be taken. It was a question whether they would prove effective. We

were abused at that time chiefly by the coal operators, the owners of the mines, and the rulings of Mr. Armstrong were not only impugned but ridiculed as leaning altogether on the side of labour. But Mr. Armstrong felt as we did, that the thing that had to be got was coal, and we got the coal. The miners acquiesced and the operators acquiesced in Mr. Armstrong's orders, and surely it is the part of wisdom now to see that the question is settled, although it is not all through yet. The difficulties are not all passed by any means. I think if the leader of the Opposition went through those mines it would not take very long to convince him that just some such system of operation and of settlement of disputes as has been installed must be continued for some little time, at all events. I do not think it would take the miners themselves long to convince him or anybody else that that is essential. What I want to impress upon the committee is this, that standing here two thousand miles away- and also in warm weather-and two years distant from the most crucial time, it is very easy to under-estimate the emergency that really confronted the Government at that time, and not only once but times almost without number. One trouble followed in the wake of another, and the very gravest apprehensions filled the minds of the people of Western Canada as to what ultimately would be the result. A government does not very often get credit for the errors that it does not commit. Here is a case where the result was as we sought, where grave danger and grave suffering were avoided by this means. The only question now is whether or not some one yet unknown is to be allowed to frustrate the good that has been done. So far as I am aware there is no question in dispute; there certainly cannot be any substantial question in dispute, and it is in the interest of the whole community that no one shall be allowed to go back and rip up the whole proceedings right from the beginning and throw the country into chaos.

The minister says that the difficulty is far from being settled and that there is still need of such legislation as was enacted by those Orders in Council. Now, Mr. Chairman, we are passing legislation here for which we shall be responsible, and we are doing it without knowing exactly what is its character. That is what I complain about. The rules of Parliament require that every piece of legislation that is passed must have three readings; the 
principle of the measure which is enacted must be discussed on the second reading and the details considered in committee, so that the public may be properly safeguarded. It is but right that this should be so, and I say that the rules of Parliament must now prevail. This country, among other misfortunes, has suffered from a dangerous disease, that of being ruled by Orders in Council. We thought that the period of such government was over, and it is over, at least so far as the determination of the people is concerned. The legislation which will be enacted in this Bill should follow the ordinary course of parliamentary enactment, and Parliament must be supreme in the future. The fact that this particular thing may have been done in the past does not alter the general principle at all. We are being told too often that the same things have happened in the past. Well, Sir, there are many people in this country at the present time, in all the provinces of Canada, and particularly among the younger generation^ that are not going to endorse and approve of things that have been done or made in the past simply because they belong to the past. The tu quoque argument is a weak one.
It is worn out.
It is a weak argument and it has never been used in so cynical a manner as this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I find no fault with the principle which the hon. member urges, but I do not see what application it has to this ease. Has this Bill not to be read three times in the Senate?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Has its principle not
been discussed on the second reading? Why, this Bill has passed through several stages. It was introduced and a debate was precipitated at that stage. It was read in the Senate a first time, a second time, and a third time.

The minister knows
very well that I am referring to the Orders in Council and not to the Bill. .

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: 1 know that, and I shall come to the point in a moment.
The Bill does not say anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It was considered in
committee in the Senate, read the third time

and passed. Here it has been introduced, read the first and second times and now is in Committee of the Whole. Now, the hon. member says that the Orders in Council have not been read. Does he want them read?

I want to read them,
surely.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, they have been
two days on the Table.
They have not been distributed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If hon. members want
to read the Orders in Council and are in earnest about it no one has ever denied them the right to do so. They have never asked for them, and if they are in earnest about wanting to read them I will not stand in their way. So what point is there in the hon. member's contention? Why, in the legislation passed before, all that was required to ratify the regulations was a resolution. All these preliminaries on which the hon. gentleman lays such stress, namely, the first, second and third readings, did not have to be gone through at all; the matter was passed by a resolution in the House. This Bill has to go through the various stages of every Bill, and while it is in progress hon. members surely have an opportunity of reading the orders of the coal director or the Orders in Council if they so desire. Consequently the indignation which my hon. friend simulates is poorly based. If he wants time to study these orders I do not think that any one is going to deny him that right; but I fancy that after he has done that he will come back in about the same disposition as he is now in, having a grievance of which there is no justification.

The answer which my hon. friend has given is his customary reply. He dances so well around a point that we see nothing; we just hear a whizz and lose sight of the point altogether. This is only quibbling. There are certain things which we have to ratify, but the substance of the Bill, which consists in 150 orders which were issued by the Fuel Controller, is not printed. My hon. friend from Quebec East has raised a point which I think is well taken. I say, Mr. Chairman, that either the Government had a right to make these orders or they did not. If they had the right to pass these Orders in Council, and there is nothing improper about the matter, why should there be any necessity for legislation now? If the orders issued by the Fuel Controller are equitable and
perfectly satisfactory, and there is nothing of which the Government need be apprehensive, what objection is there to having the whole matter freely studied? Why come before Parliament and ask hon. members to ratify orders about which they know nothing? The contention of the hon. member (Mr. Lapointe) is that the Bill does not properly present to Parliament the real purport of the legislation which we are asked to pass. We are called upon, without having had any opportunity to study them, to pass upon some 150 orders touching all sorts of subjects, and I submit that Parliament is entitled to have attached to the Bill, as so many schedules or whatever you may choose to term them, the various orders that were issued, and we ought to know precisely what they are. Is Parliament going to lay down as a principle that when the Governor in Council has authorized a man, under a measure of expediency, to do certain things, without any examination we are going to ratify what is done even though we may deprive of any redress some one who has been wronged? I think the principle is vicious and I for one cannot support it. These Orders in Council were either necessary or they were not at the time they were made. If they were necessary and the extraordinary circumstances of the time at which they were issued justified them, even though perhaps they may have been somewhat autocratic, the Government ought to have nothing to fear, and no court in the country, taking into consideration the peculiar conditions that called for them, would condemn the issuing of them. On the other hand, if a wrong was done to any one, this Parliament cannot under any circumstances commit itself to any act that will deprive that person of the right of redress. My hon. friend says that these orders have been on the Table for two days. Well, Mr. Chairman, we have been sitting here very late at night. We were here until one o'clock night before last and until midnight last night and the House now meets at two o'clock in the afternoon. Furthermore, we have been attending the Railway Committee at ten o'clock. Does my hon. friend, in view of that fact, seriously suggest that we could find time to read such a multitude of orders? It is not fair. Besides, only one copy has been tabled. These orders ought to be printed and the people should know what rules were made by the Fuel Controller; We are asked to ratify those orders now; you ask that the authority of the Fuel Controller be continued for a further period.

The orders which we are now asked to ratify were issued under Orders in Council passed in June and July in 1917 and February, 1918. At that time conditions were abnormal. The minds of the people were unsettled, and the necessity for prompt action might have existed. It is now two years since the signing of the Armistice, however, and we are asked that the Fuel Controller, who was given powers under extraordinary circumstances in a time of great emergency, shall have his authority continued for another year. There must be some reason for this. We are not in a state of war to-day, and the same emergency does not exist. Parliament is now in session, and if there are any particular cases which the minister knows of or whioh he expects may arise in the near-future why should he not inform Parliament of the fact so that we may know w'hat the authority of the Fuel Controller ought to be in these cases. I submit that the point of my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) is absolutely well taken, and that it is not an answer for the minister to say that this Bill will follow the usual procedure. What we want to analyse and to study are the orders issued and I content that the substance of those orders should be made known to the people. They ought at least to be attached, as a schedule or as exhibits, to the Bill and they ought to be discussed in committee before they are approved of.

Did not the leader of
the Opposition pay in his speech this afternoon that he would have agreed to the Government's proposition, in regard to this matter if it had not been that they proposed to carry it on for another year?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I said that
we had gone very far in allowing the first section to pass which extended the powers given the Director of Coal Operations under the several Orders in Council mentioned; that we had gone quite far enough in giving him an opportunity of continuing orders which he may have issued, but that we are going too far in seeking to legalize any orders which may not have been in accordance with the powers given him.

I would like
to be as clear as to whether the validation of this order will have any bearing whatsoever upon the powers of this official. For this purpose I see these orders are continued in operation until the end of the next session of Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the orders are in
every sense, technically, and otherwise unimpeachable they will have validity through the sustenance of the War Measures Act. But they would not after the War Measures Act had passed out of existence; consequently they would be of no value now. The Justice Department has never affirmed that as a (matter of law but the better opinion is that their validity rests upon the War Measures Act and that when that Act passes out of existence they must be renewed. It is represented that we are past the war, past the Armistice and there is not the same necessity as formerly existed. It is not more than three days since that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House drew the attention of the Government, most forcibly and rightly so, to the rather serious coal situation at the present hour. Is it well in face of that situation, that everything should fall to the ground in district 18 and that we should be precipitated back into a condition where we will have strikes instead of work, idleness instead of labour? Is it not better that we should continue that formal control which all along has been responsible for coal production in the tremendous coal area df Western Canada? That is what the Bill does. I do not find any objection to hon. gentlemen wanting every opportunity to study the orders but hon. gentlemen who resist this Bill are seeking to bring us back into that condition. That is at all events the goal towards which they are moving whether they intend to or not. It is urged that these orders should be printed as an appendix to the Bill. Why do we not do that with all regulations that are made? We would hardly be able to get the volume of our statues through the door if we were to follow that practice. These Orders in Council in themselves would make a pretty cumbersome statute. It is only right that hon. gentlemen should be able to see them to find if there is anything they can add to them. I do not believe they think they can. These orders are orders which have proved effective. Prima facie, that is sufficient for the House. If there is anything that could be called attention to, any litigation, any dispute that ought to be decided, Parliament should not get on one side or the other to the dispute. But theTe is nothing of that kind, we must ask Parliament to remove the possibility of any one, on trivial or technical grounds, tearing the whole thing down, obliging us to go way back to the beginning again and

bringing chaos and confusion. That is the only purpose of the Bill? I am introducing it as representing the 'Minister of Labour.
I do not tfhink there is any one in Canada who has as intimate a knowledge or appreciation oif the difficulties in that district as the present Minister of Labour. I do not believe that we ,could ask that this Bill be passed if we were not thoroughly convinced that it was essential to take care of the conditions now prevailing.

speechtext: We have given him poweT by section one of this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That still leaves this point: that if in any way unknown to himself-and unknown to us as far as that goes -he may have in a technical sense exceeded his powers or not particularly followed them, then some one by proceedings in court might go right hack to the whole institution of that order, throw into confusion all that has been done, and set up contentions here and contentions there that would bring the whole coal district into a state of paralysis. Anybody can see that. Consequently we want to confirm what has been done, not because it was wrong but because it has been acquiesced in, and because it is in the public interest that it should remain.

As member for a constituency which is affected by the measure which has been discussed I would say that during the period the commissioner has been in existence there has been more industrial harmony in the southern Alberta coal field than at any time previous. The mines have operated more regularly, and there has 'been less conflict between the employers and the employees than in any similar period of years in the past. It is
true that there is a difference of opinion on the part of some of the employees over some of the orders that have been issued; but I make this statement: That if there had not been any -coal commissioner in existence that -same 'trouble would have arisen, because the operators themselves, in their association and as individuals, would have demanded that similar orders apply in their mines. A rather peculiar situation has arisen. Prior to the appointment of the coal commiissioner there was a great deal of hostility on the part of the operators towards the United Mine Workers of America; but owing to difficulty that arose a few years ago, and when -there was an attempt to form a new association, the operators practically ran into the arms of the United Mine Workers and they now demand that there shall not be any other organization in the mines but it. Therefore I say that -even without the order from the coal commissioner, concerning the United Mine Workers, that -has been mentioned the operators would have demanded the same thing even if they -had been operating apart from the commissioner altogether.
I-t must be remembered that this order does not apply to all the coal mines in the province of Alberta. It only . applies-I think I am safe in saying this-to the mines within the Operators' Association, because I know of a mine in the Taber field east of the city of Lethbridge, that is not under the control of the coal commissioner. The mines within the Operators' Association are under his control. Now what has happened under the rule of the coal commissioner? We had very little trouble in the coal fields of Alberta at the beginning of the winter season-in the late fall and the early winter. I only know of one case since the coal commissioner was appointed where there was serious trouble in the mines. That was over an order that was issued affecting the mines of' British Columbia, but that particular trouble, according to my recollection, did not take place during the critical season. There has been under this system an assurance of a coal supply that was not guaranteed to us in the years before the coal commissioner was appointed. I confidently assert that the mines have operated more regularly during the last four years than they have ever operated before, and there has been less conflict of opinion than previously over the question of wages. What has happened in connection with the question of wages? There was an investigation under this

system, in regard to the cost of living in the communities where the mines operate, and as a result of that inquiry an increase was granted to the employees in nearly every case, and I think I am safe in saying that the miners themselves were satisfied with that increase. The chief difficulty over any orders that have been issued have been in regard to hours and in regard to the recognition of a certain union; but I repeat that that difficulty would have existed even if there had not- been a coal commissioner, because the Operators' Association itself was determined that only one main organization would be recognized in those mines, and even in the absence of a coal commissioner they would have demanded that that union should be recognized. I do not think we could have overcome that difficulty by the coal commissioner not issuing any order in that connection. The difficulty in Alberta is peculiar to that province, and is a conflict between two groups of men in the labour world. The operators are strongly in favour of one organization, and there is a group of men who are in favour of another. It is true that the commissioner interfered and Issued an order that dealt with that particular situation, but even if he had not done so, even if he had refrained from dealing with the situation, the operators would still have persisted in their demand that that particular union be recognized.
On the whole I am not disputing the points that have been raised, particularly by the leader of the Opposition, in order to give full publicity to these orders. What I am saying is that according to my experience and my knowledge-coming as I do from a coal field that is largely affected by this legislation-there has been more peace and harmony since we have had a coal commissioner than there was prior to the appointment of that official.
Another point I would like to make is this: Usually when there is hostility to legislation that is being introduced into Parliament we hear about it both from the miners and the operators. This Bill has been discussed in the Senate, it is generally known that it is before Parliament, and I have not received one single protest from a miners union or from an operator in my constituency or in Southern Alberta.

I listened with the very greatest care to the arguments on this clause. With regard to what I would call giving this official reasonable legislative sanctuary from acts taken in the emergencies of war I think the argument of

the Government would carry me along with them. I do not think that it would be wise to leave an official, who acted under the pressure of war conditions, liable eighteen months after the Armistice to litigation now that the war has happily ended in our favour.
With regard to the continuance of these powers my mind, I must say, till an advanced period of the debate was in doubt. I think the committee knows what my general attitude is on this question. The sooner we get away from boards, controllers, commissions and other things appointed in war time, as a general principle, the better; but perhaps one needs to add that the sooner people get quite sane again the better. I cannot help thinking and feeling that the continued existence of these abnormal controls is an irritant upon the public mind. In Anglo-Saxon countries we have been used to live in an atmosphere of freedom, and as a general principle I do-not recede from that point. However, I have a very large amount of faith in my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan), and I must say that I have been tremendously impressed by what has just fallen from him. Here is an hon. gentleman living in the locality where these troubles have existed, and where they might exist again, who tells us that the operations of the commissioner and the state of affairs that existed during the war and up to, the present time have led to the greatest harmony in that country that- he has ever known. Well, Mr. Chairman, I for one would have very great hesitation at this juncture in voting that we should run any risk in this matter. For some period during seven successive months last winter we had zero temperature in that province. That is the time when coal is needed, and I should hesitate in taking any steps which would, as my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior put it, perhaps throw the whole business into a state of chaos. If this question comes to a vote I shall therefore with a clear conscience be compelled to support the Government.

My hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) argues that the coal controller has become necessary. If so,, and he is to become a permanent official, why should not this Parliament pass legislation defining his powers? This is not . the proper way to do it. The war time is-over. These Orders in Council were passed to meet emergencies arising during the war. If we find that the experimnest we made at

that time to meet emergencies ought to be continued, let us cut out the Orders in Council and bring in an Act of Parliament providing that a fuel controller shall be appointed, and defining his powers.
Let us get back to normal.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the Government were convinced that this was a permanent situation clearly it would be the act of wisdom to adopt the course my hon. friend suggests; but the Government is not so convinced. We feel that it is essential to hold the situation for the time being and leave Parliament next session either to legislate its permanence or to let it go out of existence. For myself, I hope the latter course will be possible-a hope that I am sure is shared by every hon. member. But surely the right thing to do now is merely to hold on and leave Parliament free.

I made the statement that the operations of the Coal Commissioner applied only to the operators within the Coal Operators' Association. I have heard the statement made that the commissioner had power to rule that the operators of a mine that did not want to be linked up with the Coial Operators' Association, and did not want to comply with his orders, must accept his orders. But my understanding is that his orders apply only to the mines that are within the Association, not to all mines in the province of Alberta.

I think my hon. friend is mistaken as to that. By a subsequent Order in Council the jurisdiction of Mr. Armstrong was extended to take in all the mines in province of Alberta and in that portion of British Columbia between the easterly border and the summit of the Rocky Mountains.
IMr. BUCHANAN: I might point out that some operators of mines that have been in the Coal Operators' Association for a number of years broke away from it either last spring or late this winter and were acting independently of the Association. I know of one mine, the Western Canada Coal Company at Tabor, where the men were not expected to fulfil the order as to joining a particular union; it was practically an open shop, and if the men organized another union they were allowed to join it. Seemingly they were not affected by this order. I would make this statement from my knowledge, that the order has not been applied in the way that is mentioned here, that is, to all the mines in the province of Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To district 18.

Some of the mine
operators have been willing to accept this order, among others the operators association. There are other mines in the province that did not come under that order at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The order was apparently made to apply on the 20th of February, 1918, to all coal mines and coke producing plants situated in the province of Alberta and also those in the province of British Columbia eastward from the summit of the Rocky Mountains.

My point is that I do not think the Coal Commissioner should be given such drastic powers as to compel a mine operator to do something that he does not want to do in respect to the employment of men. If he can operate his mine successfully with certain men, although they do not belong to a union, he should be allowed to do it. The coal operators belonging to the Association are agreeable to the order that has been issued, and I am speaking of those outside the Association.
IMr. CROTHERS: I think I am speaking within the mark, Mr. Chairman, when I advise my hon. friend that the Director of Coal Operations never interfered where the employer and the employee at any particular mine got on agreeably.
