speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways) the House went into Committee

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
on Bill No. 141, respecting Canadian National Railways, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
On section 1-short title:

I have not had an opportunity to study this Bill very closely. If we are Building and extending lines in the West, what are the chances of their paying? Will they pay any better than the roads that the Government are now running?

This is the Bill which was referred to the Railway Committee a few days ago. Charters are being asked for the extension of three lines, one is from Prince Albert north; another from a. point near the American border, and the third an extension of what we call the Turtleford Branch. The mileage in each case as about fifty miles. The extensions are to provide newly settled districts with necessary railway facilities. Hon. gentlemen will remember that when the legislation respecting the Canadian National Railways was put through it was understood that no further extension should be carried' out or no new lines built in connection with the Canadian National Railways without charters being first granted by Parliament. This is not to provide for the building of some new line that has not been considered before; it is simply to provide for these three small extensions. Probably about half the work will be done on each of the three extensions this year.

Since my hon. friend is going to provide for the building of extensions amounting to about 150 miles in the West, I want to take advantage of the'oppor-tunity to ask him not to forget that very little line of three miles, practically a siding, which is necessary to connect the town of Lockeport, in the county of Shelburne, with the main railway line. I may use the words that my hon. friend has used: this is not something new or unknown; the line which is needed is simply an extension of three miles in order to reach the centre of population at Lockeport. I do not want to say more than to ask the minister to give the matter consideration.

While the minister is on the subject of the extension of railways, I wish to direct his atention to a matter which I believe has been already favourably considered,-that of the building of a short line of railway in New Brunswick to connect the Canadian National Railway system in the Maritime Provinces and Eastern Quebec with the Maine Central, which is our natural outlet from the Maritime Provinces. Practically three-quarters of the freight that originates on the Canadian
[Mr. Meighen.l
National railway in the Maritime Provinces and Eastern Quebec is destined for the New England States. To-day we have either to pay the Canadian Pacific a large toll,-they have the connecting link between the Canadian National railways
4 p.m. and the Maine Central-or ship, via the north shore of New Brunswick, which is a very long route indeed. The route to which 1 refer has been surveyed. The line would be 22 miles long, and I believe that the estimated cost of construction is $1,000,000. But the line would pay for itself in ten years, if not less. Moreover, the St. John and Quebec railway, which the Government took over recently and are operating, is carrying on at quite a heavy loss every year. If this connecting link was built, all the freight originating on the Canadian National railways in the Maritime Provinces would be routed over the St. John and Quebec railway 'to reach this connecting line, so that the St. John and Quebec railway would be made a paying instead of a losing proposition. The building of this short line would be a good proposition from the point of view of the Government. I know that money is scarce and that we are all talking economy, and, I hope, trying to practice it. At the same time, it is often more economical to spend money that will bring you a return than not to spend it at all. While I do not know the merits of the lines proposed to be extended under this Bill, I do know the merits of this line which I am now advocating, and I think that the minister knows them as well. I hope that while he is on this subject he will give this matter very earnest consideration.

I am familiar with the proposal to which my hon. friend (Mr. Caldwell) refers. About four years ago it was suggested that he Government should build that connecting line; it was shown that its construction would result in a great saving in the matter of traffic originating in the lower province and destined to the Eastern States. On account of the financial situation, action was delayed. There is no doubt that the construction of this line should be carried out. But just at present the people in that district are not suffering actual lack of transportation facilities, though they may have to pay a little more for freight. The Canadian Pacific as well as the Canadian National Railway Company will for some years be compelled to build extensions of lines in the western provinces. People are going into unsettled districts forty or fifty miles

from the railway, on the 'basis of the promise or the expectation that railways will go into that part of the country. It is a new country; we are trying to get settlers there, and we imust provide them with railway facilities at the earliest possible moment. I have no doubt at all that when we ge't back to normal conditions the Government will take up a scheme such as the one suggested and deal rwith these matters in the way that it is practically understood by the department and the railway officials that they should be carried out.

I was under the impression that the Canadian Northern had gone .out of existence when the Government took over the property, but here we find the name cropping up again. This Bill is to empower the Canadian Northern to build branch lines. Who are the directors of this company that is called the Canadian Northern Railway Company?

The incorporation of
the Canadian National Railway system does not put out of existence the Canadian Northern Railway. Its stock will be transferred to the Canadian National Railway system when the necessary Order in 'Council has been passed, but the Canadian Northern will still be kept alive. It will be a subsidiary company of the Canadian National Railway system. The directors of the Canadian Northern are the directors of the Canadian National Railway system. Their names have already been given to the House but I will try and recall them to my hon. friend: D. G. Hanna, President, A. J. Mitchell, Vice-President, Mr. Graham Bell, Sir Hormisdas Laporte, Mr. Riley of Winnipeg, Mr. Hobson of Hamilton, Mr. E. R. Wood of Toronto, Mr. Cantley of Nova Scotia, and Mr. Barnhill of New Brunswick.

Those are the directors
of the Canadian National Railways.

It is the same thing.
They are also the directors of the Canadian Northern. Whoever are the directors of the Canadian National Railway will be the directors of all the subsidiary companies when we bring into force by Order in Council the legislation which has been passed regarding these railways.
Who appoints these directors?

They are appointed by the shareholders. The Canadian Government appoints them for the people. Whoever the Government names for the directors of the subsidiary companies are appointed at the annual meeting.

Was there any special
reason why we should say in this legislation the Oandian Northern Railway Company instead of the Canadian National Railways?

These are really extensions to the Canadian Northern Railway, which owns the road running through that particular part of the country. We have in Nova Scotia, for instance, the Halifax and Southwestern Railway, a subsidiary of the Canadian Northern. The stock of that railway is all owned by the Canadian Northern and will be owned by the Canadian National Railway system, but if we wanted to build an extension of fifteen miles to the Halifax and Southwestern railway we would ask for an extension for that particular railway, not for an extension of the Canadian National Railway system.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Inasmuch as on this Bill the minister has (widened out the scope of inquiry to include the Canadian National Railways, may I ask that when he brings down his Estimates he be prepared to make a statement to the House of the amounts paid to each transportation company for the carrying of mails from Halifax, St. John, N. B., Quebec, Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg to points west and in the case of all except Halifax also to points east.
If the information can be got out in that form I will give instructions this afternoon to my department and the Post Office Department to have it prepared.
Do I understand that the minister is building new lines of railway in the West ?

These are not new railways, but extensions to present lines.
Mr. 'SINCLAIR (Guysborough): My hon. friend will remember that there is a railway in Eastern Nova Scotia about which representations have been made to him for many years. At the present time twelve miles of that railway have been completed and are in operation, and the whole question now is in regard to the extension of the railway, in which some 40,000 people are interested. Some families have lived ini that part of the country since the American revolution and are still without railway accommodation. My hon. friend is anxious and rightly so, to provide railway accommodation for new settlers in Western Canada,

but I would also urge upon him that the old settlers, some of whom and their forefathers have been in this country for 150 years are also entitled to some consideration. Does my hon. friend think it is more important to extend railways in Western Canada to give accommodation to new settlers than to extend railways in the part of Nova Scotia to which I have referred to accommodate the large population who hafve occupied that country for so many generations?

I would not say that it is more necessary to provide railway accommodation for new settlers in Western Canada than for the people the hon, member speaks for. I am not as familiar with the situation in that part of the country as my hon. friend, tout if they have been without railway accommodation for so long a time as he says, and it is so urgently required the hon. member should have got it for them during the seventeen years he sat in this House as a supporter of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and then he would not be appealing to me to-day. I have had no one pressing me for a railway in that particilar locality. As to these extensions in Western Canada, there is no doubt at all that the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk as well, I suppose, promised branch lines to the people who settled in the western provinces. Furthermore, we have encouraged immigration to this country for many years. We have been advertising the fact that in our western provinces there was a great field for immigrants to come and settle. All Governments, not simply the present Government, tout the previous government, and the Government before that, have encouraged settlers to come to Canada and have promised them railway accommodation if they will settle there. Having promised these people that we would build railways as fast as settlement justified it, I feel that we should carry out that promise. The Canadian Pacific are certainly carrying out that very policy. I feel that when it is shown to us that settlement has progressed to such an extent that it will pay to build a railway to allow these settlers to get out their wheat and other products, the railway accommodation should be provided.

My hon. friend is right in saying that in Eastern Nova Scotia we should have got this railway built while the late Government was in power, but he has not told the whole story. During those years there was great

opposition on the part of both political parties to undertaking the construction of branch lines anywhere on the Intercolonial railway. During the period that the Conservative party were in power prior to 1896, the attitude of the Government was that they could not afford to begin to build these branch lines. I believe the reason generally given was that if they commenced to do so they would be swamped with applications. There was therefore no branch line policy adopted by either party up to the year 1910. In 1910 when a resolution was brought forward by my late hon. friend from the county of Westmorland, Mr. Emerson, the Government of that day accepted it and adopted the policy of building branch lines for the-first time. Immediately after that, at the very next session of Parliament, provision was made for those branch lines I refer to. It was acknowledged on all sides that the Guysborough branch should be the first to be built. A million dollars was voted in 1911, immediately after Die decision had been arrived at by Parliament to begin the construction of branch lines on the Intercolonial. A contract was then made tj build that line. Tenders were called for, surveys were made and two branch lines were projected, one in the county of Halifax and one in the counties of Guysborough and Pictou. Another was projected in the island of Cape Breton, of which my hon. friend who sits near me (Mr. McKenzie) has often spoken. Advertisements were published and tenders were received, and a million dollars was provided by Parliament for the building of each of these branch lines. Then, when the business was at that stage, there was a change of government. The county of Halifax was represented by the .Prime Minister and one of his colleagues, not now in this House, and the county of Guysborough by your humble servant. The contracts were exactly similar, a million dollars having been voted for each. They were executed at the same time and everything was done before the change of Government took place. Thereafter, what happened? The Government repudiated the contract for the building of the branch line into the county of Guysborough but continued the contract 'or the railway into the country represented by the Prime Minister. It is not creditable to the Government that they should have treated one county differently from another simply because the county of Guysborough happened to be represented by a member of the Opposition. That is what happened, however, and I had hoped that my hon. friend would have redeemed the

record and wiped out the reproach of the Government. He has not done so. I have on various occasions obtained hopeful promises from my hon. friend that he would reconsider this matter. I quite understand that it is difficult at the present time to get money to build railways anywhere, but if railways are to be built I submit that there is no part of Canada where the need is so urgent as in that locality. There are great natural resources to he developed there; there are great fishing, lumber and mining industries, and that part of the country has been kept back all these years because this railway has not been built. There is no other way of obtaining railway facilities for this locality except as a branch of the Government railways, because it is _ not possible as a commercial enterprise to build short branch lines such as this. I submit that my hon. friend should now deal with this question. I would not press it at the present time were it not for the fact that he is building railways in other parts of Canada; and when he undertakes to construct railways in Western Canada for new settlers who have been in the country only a short time, and denies the same right to people who have been here for generations, I think it is eminently unfair and the Government cannot defend such a policy. I contend that they cannot fairly build new railways in Western Canada if they refuse to do the same thing for Eastern Canada.

I agree with the proposal to make these three extensions provided for in this Bill. The hon. member (Mr. Sinclair) speaks about new localities that are now being served by these railways. The locality that is being provided for by No. 3 has been longer settled than the district in Nova Scotia to which my hon. friend referred. Thirty-five years ago Willow Bunch and Wood Mountain districts were among the oldest settlements in the country. The settlers have lived there for years and years and have to cart their produce thirty, forty and fifty miles to the nearest centre. There is another thing that makes the third line necessary. It runs within five or six miles of the international boundary line and the settlers there are largely American in sentiment and during the past number of years have been taking all their produce across to the United States. They have been taking all their wheat and other things and selling it there and doing all their purchasing on the American side. As I said in the Railway Committee the other day, so far as these two tiers of townships along the
Montana boundary line are concerned they might as well be in the United States, for they are not a part of Canada as regards their trade. We can only expect that condition to continue so long as they are nearer the American railway than the Canadian, and the only way in which we can make these two townships a real part of Canada is by giving them the railway facilities they so much need. I trust therefore that not only will these railways be built as quickly as possible, but that it will be a settled policy that the line shall be continued further west from year to year until the whole of the townships abutting Montana are served by the Canadian railways and brought into touch with Canadian centres. There is one thing that has puzzled me and I should like the minister to make a statement on the point. Is it his intention, or does he promise, that these three branches will not only be graded but will be steeled this year? I ask this question because last year we provided for a branch line further east running from Peebles to Lampman for a distance of some twenty miles and we were hoping that it would be built this year because it taps a magnificent coal mine which we want to reach. Although the Government has made all provision necessary in the way of charter, money, etc., I find by a letter that I received the other day from the manager of the Canadian National Railways that they will not be able to complete it this year because they cannot get the steel. How can they get steel for these three branches and not for a branch already authorized? I contend that the line already started should be finished and steeled before further extensions are made, because the one already authorized is a very important one to the people of the city of Regina and to thousands of people who want to get this coal. A company with $500,000 capital is now operating and it is completely stuck because it is eight miles away from a railway. This branch has been promised and these people are waiting for it. I would like to know if the steel is going to be provided for this road this year?

In reference to the question of doing grading work and providing steel for these three branch lines, and also why we did not put the steel on this Willow Bunch-Wood Mountain, line last year. I may say that in the first of the year the board of directors lay down their construction policy for the year. That was done last year and it was decided that 350 miles was

the outside limit that could be constructed. Parliament voted the money necessary to do the work on 350 miles. But there is no use of saying that we can guarantee to build 350 miles. If we cannot get the rails, ties and labour we cannot do the work. We were not able to do the 350 miles because we could not get the labour or the rails. This year we have laid down a construction policy of about 350 miles. The Canadian Pacific have also laid down a construction policy of 350 miles. Early in the year they believed they could do that amount of work and we believed we could do the same. But there is a shortage of labour and of rails. Every effort is being made by the Government and the Canadian Pacific to get the labour necessary to complete the 350 miles. If we can get the rails we will complete all we decided to do last year. That will have the preference in so far as the rails are concerned. Then we will follow that up with 350 miles that we have decided to go ahead with this year if we can get the rails and labour. Part of this mileage is included in the three lines I am now asking charters for. The charters are for about fifty miles each or 150 miles in all. We do not intend to grade or lay the rails on the 150 miles this year but probably 15 or 20 miles of each of these three lines is all we can expect to do this year. Contracts for grading will be let and tenders are now waiting for these charters to be put through. If we can get the rails and the men, which we are trying to arrange for now, we will have the steel laid and the grading done on 15 or 20 miles of each of these branch lines.
Can the Minister tell us what is the population of the district traversed by these railways?

Parties from these
localities stated what the population was in the Railway Committee the other day. They said that there were large settlements in each district. In the Prince Albert district there is a population of 40,000. A large population has been settled there for some time and( there has been a very largely signed petition from all the people in the locality. We have also had deputations to the Government and the board of management not only this year but lost year urging the -construction of these roads.

I was in the Railway Committee the other day and I did not hear any one say what the population was in the

territories that these railways will traverse. vVhen the hon. member at the back of the Minister suggests to him that there are
40,000	people, it shows a woeful lack of accurate information because there are not more than 40,000 people in the whole district of Prince Albert which is already served by two large railways. The country is well served to the -South and the only question it as to the North. That is an indication of the kind of information we are getting here in regard to the railway situation. I want to bring to the attention of the Government what appears to be the most important matter in connection with the whole question. That is:	who recommends the construction of these railways? Is it recommended by the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways? If so, what promises have been made to the Government as to the possibility of earning a revenue on these extensions? What promises have been made to the Government as to their ability to pay the interest on this investment? Before we get too deep into this proposition I would like to remind the Minister of Railways that the Minister of Finance on the ISth day of May informed the House that he had practically written off $140,000,000 of advances to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. What were the advances for? For the construction of railways, for the building of branch lines and such work, I presume, because it is stated that the whole amount is represented by assistance furnished by this Government to the Canadian Northern. Where do we get to by this policy? What is the policy? We are at both ends of this question. We are representing the people who owned the Canadian Northern railway. Our directors on the one hand come to us and say: "We want to build certain branch lines". We, on the other hand, represent the people who must pay and we are entitled to ask the directors, or the Government:	"What
do you expect to accomplish by building these branch lines?" This is no longer a philanthropic proposition. We are not in a position to continuously hand out money to these people. What is the policy of this railway, company? What is the' policy of the Government in regard to the railway question? Are we going to build where the greatest pressure is brought to bear? Are we going to build along the boundary line because somebody is selling his wheat and buying his sugar in the United States, or because somebody is trading with the United

States? We are trading with every country in the world. Surely that is no excuse for building a railway. We are not going to build railways to stop people from trading with the United States. We want to know whither we are heading? AVe cannot go on indefinitely spending money with one hand and having the Minister of Finance coming down and writing off the investment with the other. The people of the whole of Canada are paying for these railways. Each district throughout Canada will want its pro rata share of its construction of railways. It is all very well for the Minister to say that these railways are going to earn interest but the man who is in a position to give us an opinion says that this investment is a bad asset and that these railways are not in a position to earn interest. He writes it off, dismisses it and no longer counts it as an asset. How much longer are we going to continue this policy? Have you determined on what ground you are building these western lines? Is it on the ground that pressure is being brought to bear for their construction. AVhat kind of pressure is it-political or otherwise? Is it on the ground that this section of country will develop traffic that will earn money tfor the railway company or is the motive purely political? This committee is entitled to know where we are heading for and what we are driving at in regard to this 360 or more miles of railway that the Minister talks so freely about building this year. We should understand where we are heading for. The minister and his colleagues in the Cabinet should sit down and come to some conclusion about this railway policy. They should adopt a railway policy. They should have a real railway policy before they come and ask for charters to build more railways when they have absolutely no idea as to where the money to pay for those railways is coming from other than it is coming out of the pockets of the already heavily burdened taxpayers of Canada. In the absence of exact information this is not a good, sound, proposition. The Government should ask themselves these questions: Is it necessary toi build these roads? It may be necessary to open up the territory in question, but would some private railway company build the lines required to serve that territory? Is that territory so valuable that if the Government lines were extended into it the result would be to yield such dividends as would help to reduce the existing deficit? We have not had any information with
respect to, these lines in the railway committee, that is any dependable figures with respect to the territory proposed to be served and the population which it contains. AVhen these charters came up in the railway committee, for example, no member, not even the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) could give a rough estimate of the number of people that wolld be advantaged by the line running north of the city of that name. Neither did any person attempt to give an estimate of the population in the \A7illow Buttes district, or in the district being served by the line running northwest from Radisson. It is not only that we are asked to grant these charters. As a matter of fact we have to. find the money with which to build the railways in question. Can it be that the Government <are so callous, and so used to doing things that no person with a conscience would attempt to do, that they propose to go ahead without furnishing the detailed information that is necessary? 1 can tell them that the time will come when they will be answerable to the people; their mandate has long since expired. They will soon have to account for their deeds and will have to make fitting explanation to the people. I repeat the Government of this country should have a policy regarding the railway situation. I venture to say that not a man in this committee has asked what the expenditure per mile is going to be in connection with these branch railways. I asked that question in the railway committee, but I only received an evasive reply. I was told the cost might be $30,000, or $35,000, and even $45,000. The Government really have no correct conception of what the construction of these lines is going to cost, or where they are going to get the necessary money to build them-dn fact they do not know where they are heading for.

The hon. member is
afraid there is some political move behind the construction of these railways, but he need not he worried to the extent of one particle in that regard. The Government have a policy, and that policy has been explained not only in this House but in the , railway committee as well. The hon. member wants to know whether these lines will pay if they are built. Let me tell him that the Government do not intend to build one mile of railway until it has been shown aud demonstrated to them that it will pay. The policy of constructing railways that will parallel1 other lines, or en-

croach upon the territory which the existing lines already serve while it has been one that has been followed by all Governments ever since Confederation has been discontinued so far as the present Government is concerned. They will only build such lines, or agree to their extension, when it has been shown that they will pay. Now let me demonstrate to the hon. member that so far as the Canadian Northern railway is concerned there would not- be any possible chance of its paying in the West unless it were furnished with these branch lines.
Which branch lines?

All the branch lines
in connection with the Canadian Northern railway, feeders to the main line. In the case' of these particular fifteen miles of line, the products of the territory through which they will pass will be such as to well pay the main line for their carriage. Let me say to the hon. member that in the three western provinces not only the main lines but the branch lines of the Canadian Northern already in existence, have always paid. They paid last year, they will pay this year, and they will continue to pay. The loss on the operation of the Canadian Northern was owing to the several governments concerned allowing them to build a railway westward from Port Arthur where there were no feeders; but the lines to which I have alluded have always paid and will continue to pay. The hon. member was present in the railway committee, and heard the discussion there. He will therefore agree with me that the policy determined upon of building these branch lines is fair, just and right, and that when the lines are constructed they will greatly add to the success and profit of the main systems of which they will be feeders.

The Minister has stated
that the Canadian Northern railways in the West, both main line and branch, have always paid?
Yes.

Then I presume he will
be able to substantiate that statement when the railway estimates are up for consideration.

If the hon. member is not willing to accept the statement of the Minister of Railways, perhaps he will accept the statement of the Hon. Charles Dunning, Liberal minister, in the province of Saskatchewan. That province has guaranteed

millions of dollars-I do not know how many million-for the construction of branch lines in connection with the different railways of that province, and Mr. Dunning stated, within the last year that he would not be at all sorry if he had to take over all those branch lines that had been so guaranteed because every one was a paying investment. The authority of a Liberal minister in a Liberal Government ought to be sufficient authority for the Liberal member of Pontiac.
Mr. CAHILL. That fact would go a long way to recommend them, but it is not a question of somebody thinking or saying so. The facts should be available, and all I want is that the facts- be produced before the committee showing the earnings of the main line throughout the western country and of the extensions that have been built.

There is one feature in
connection with this matter which the minister has brought up, and it is this: Reference has been made to the directorate of the Canadian Northern Railway. Now as far as this railway is concerned we find that every year we are going into the hole about 550,000,000 and that all our other railway securities-

No. I am saying that the Government railways are going into the hole about $50,000,000. I want to point out to the minister something very serious that the people of this country have taken into their consideration in connection with this matter. In the United States, in the case of every great railway, the executive officers and directors -are composed of railway operators, men who understand their business. The presidents, vice-presidents, and directors are all men who are experts in their line of business. But this Government railway is managed by a lot of men that I consider are nothing but political profiteers. They are merchants and brokers, and men who sell coal to the Government, and I think the time has come when that has got to stop. Further, I have got to say this-and I am speaking, perhaps, on behalf of the East rather than of the West-I think the time has come when this quarrel between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Government railways should end. Because a

few of the officials of our Government system and the minister have a quarrel with the Canadian Pacific Railway, that is no Teason why the people should have to make up a deficit of $50,000,000 a year. The people are demanding that the minister shall put our Government railways on a paying basis within a few months' time. And that is a very easy thing to do. It is only a question of increasing the rates. Why should we have to continue paying annual deficits of $50,000,000 unless the Government want to make public ownership of railways unpopular? I am speaking on behalf of public ownership. I think we cannot avoid it, and the only proper course to pursue is to see that our national railways are made to pay. Any business man inside *of twenty-four hours could arrange a tariff by which those railways could be put on a profitable basis, and we would not be confronted every year with these deficits. It is a black mark against the financial reputation otf this country that those deficits should occur year after year, and it influences other nations against us in so far as our credit is concerned.
With regard to the building of branch lines in the West, that is a question which the minister has fully considered. He has explained, and it is no doubt true, that the branch lines of cur national system in the West are paying. But so far as the East is concerned any further building of branch lines would to a large extent be merely a needless duplication. I am sorry that the hon. gentleman who referred to a certain branch line in Nova Scotia is not in hiis seat.
He is.

Oh, yes, I see him now.
I have a distinct recollection of a charter being granted for that railway in 1908, when a carload otf Wheelbarrows and shovels was taken up there on the eve of the election just so that he and his friends could carry the riding; and the same thing occuired in 1911. He and his colleague were two of the strongest men in this House from Nova Scotia, and if they had had any real intention of building that railway they could have done so between 1908 and 1911. But, Mr. Chairman, that charter was obtained purely for political purposes, and for that reason I think the Minister of Railways before going ahead with any such branch line would be well advised to take into consideration the local conditions. Of course, if he wanted to carry the riding 215
against the hon. gentleman at the next election he might go down there and have a carload of shovels and wheelbarrows dumped on the location on the eve otf the election.
That would not be sufficient.

Then the story might be
repeated that he would not come back. But that branch line has been purely a political venture, and I think it is a great waste of time to deal with it here.
This question of seeing that our national railways pay for themselves is a very vital question, and the only way to make them pay is to increase the freight rates. So far as I have heard there is but one argument advanced against such an increase:	That
the Canadian Pacific railway would benefit. Well, there are methods by which that could be prevented. But even if the Canadian Pacific railway did make some money out of an increase in freight rates, what about it? The Canadian Pacific railway is one of our foremost institutions, its credit and standing are international, and at the present moment its securities are lower than they have ever been for the last fifteen years. That does not speak well for this country in our period of reorganization when we need more population and more capital. But the tide of immigration has entirely stopped, and although the statistics for the last few months are not yet available, I think I am safe in saying that we have been losing rather than gaining population If we are going to make this country attractive to immigrants we must reduce taxation, and we cannot do that if every year the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) asks us to make good a $50,000,000 deficit on the operation of our national railways. That condition of affairs prejudices us in the eyes of the world, and naturally it is said: Oh, Canada is a poor country. Look at its Government railways comprising over 20,000 miles, they are in a hole every year to the extent of $40,000,000 or $50,000,000. The people of this country are now demanding that the Minister of Railways of this or any other Government shall see to it that the deficits on the operation of our national railway system are changed into surpluses. I have no quarrel with the minister about building branch lines. No doubt he has figures to show whether or not those branch lines will pay. I am speaking of the whole system. There must be a change in management, new men must be put in charge and held strictly responsible for the profit-



able and efficient operation of the system. Any business man would demand that the system be operated so as to show a surplus rather than a deficit. The Government has it in his own hands to make public ownership of railways a success, for it can control freight rates, and it is absolutely contrary to public policy that we should continue to operate our national railways at rates which entail steady and increasing losses. Those who use our railways for the shipment of thousands of tons of freight should not ask our working men and factory girls to make up that deficit; they should be prepared to meet it by paying freight rates which will not only cover the cost of operation but leave a profit for the benefit of the Treasury.
I think the Minister of Railways should be ready at- an early date to assure this Chamber that he is putting his house in order, and that the rates are to Ibe immediately increased to a paying basis. There is no quarrel with the Canadian Pacific railway, there is not quarrel with public ownership, which will justify these continued deficits, and the time has come when the Parliament of Canada, irrespective of political affiliations, should put its foot firmly down and say:	We must have an
end of these deficits, and there must be a new form of management to bring that about.
Mr. Chairman-

speechtext: ' To the branch lines mentioned in the present Bill.

I can speak for the branch lines in the northern part of the three prairie provinces. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) stated that the branch lines of our national system in the West were a paying proposition; in that statement he is absolutely correct. It is a fact that about a month ago the grain crop of last year was not moved out of Northern Saskatchewan on lines tributatry to the Canadian National system, and if our National railways are to be made to pay they must be fed by branch lines in the -most productive part of the Dominion, and that is the northern part of the prairie provinces. I do not know about conditions in the East, and therefore I shall confine my remarks to that part of the West with which I am familiar. I have this information from a railway official, that if we have this year a normal grain crop in Western Canada we will have the biggest grain blockage that we have ever experienced in that country.
It is time for the Minister of Railways to get the necessary rolling stock and have the road beds put in first class condition, so that when the crop goes on the market our railway system, branch lines as well as main lines, will be able to keep the traffic moving. If this is not done, there is no use in our building branch lines. I am prepared to give the Government and the Minister of Railways my hearty support in the construction of branch lines on the Canadian National Railway system in Western Canada

wherever they are needed. Branch lines must be constructed if we are to reach the outlying settlements and give those who settle in our country a chance to get their produce to the market.
Mr. Chairman-
Question.

Oh no, we are not ready for the question. Hon. members opposite make their speeches, and when it comes to somebody else's turn they say: ''Question". Just as much time will be saved and just as much progress will be made if hon. gentlemen show some degree of fairness and if the minister lets everybody have his say. II do not propose at this time of my life to be turned off as easily as hon. gentlemen may think when I have some remarks to make.	-

I take issue with the
hon. member. I have no objection if he takes a week on this Bill. But he knows that the Estimates must come up and that on those Estimates the general railway policy may be discussed. If, however, he wishes to take up the time of the committee in discussing a matter which is really not before us, I am willing that he do so; hon. members may take up as much time as they like in a discussion of the whole railway policy.

The minister spoke on this Bill; the member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) spoke on it, as did the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill); the member for Regina (Mr. Cowan); the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie). All made long speeches along lines of a general character. Now, when the member for North Cape Breton and Victoria wants to speak, it is alleged that he is improperly taking up the time of the committee. That is the ruling of the minister.
No, it is not the ruling of the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. That was not
the ruling of the minister; it was the ruling of the Chairman. The hon. member who was called to order was not the member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), but the member for Mackenzie (M. J. F. Reid), who had the floor when the ruling was given. I am sorry that the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria should be deprived of the opportunity of making his speech, and once more I am willing to ask for the unanimous eon-215J
sent of the committee that he be allowed to make that speech. But if the Chairman remained seated and allowed each member of the committee to make the same kind of speech as that made by each of the hon. members mentioned a moment ago by the member for North Cape Breton and Victoria, the Chairman would certainly not be doing his duty.
Some hon.-MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

I am not finding fault with the ruling. There was a time in my life when I presided in a court, and if a lawyer tried to give me law that was bad I would tell him so at once; I would not let him waste a whole day in giving 5 p.m. bad law. With all due deference, I submit that when we begin to drift from the proper line, the thing to do is to stop it at .once, and not give an advantage to half a dozen members to make their speeches before shutting another member off. I stand by the ruling, but 1 submit that the ruling should be made whenever the digression occurs. 'I have no desire to depart from the rules, but I think there is necessity for information in connection with this Bill. The minister has said that no action was taken until there was assurance that the building of these extensions would be a business proposition. What assurance has the Government to that effect? What survey has: been made? Is the minister in possession of a report from Mr. Hanna? Is there a report from the (Chief Engineer giving the assurance that this is a business proposition and that there will be no loss to the people if they put their money into this new venture?

Before the board decided to ask for these charters they had their officials go over the territory with a view to seeing whether these lines should- be built. Mr. M. H. MacLeod, assistant to Mr. Hanna,-in fact, the gentleman who laid out the whole of the Canadian Northern lines in Western Canada-is in charge of extensions and the construction of lines in that part of the country. Hon. members who have been in the West will agree that the Canadian National or Canadian Northern lines in the West are well located and are all on a paying basis. Now, Mr. MadLeod, with his staff, examined this territory and recommended, in his report to the management, that these extensions be made. Mr. MacLeod and his engineering staff came to Ottawa and I went over the whole matter with them. Subsequently a

sub-committee of the Cabinet, composed of Sir Henry Drayton, Mr. Calder and myself, went to Toronto and discussed the extensions proposed to be made during the coming year. Only after we spent two days in Toronto with Mr. Hanna, Mr. Mitchell, Mr. MacLeod, Mr. Hungerford and other officials did we come to the conclusion that the extensions now proposed were not only necessary and in the public interest,	but	should	be proceededwith at	the	earliest	possible day.
I only mention this to show that we are not going on with this work simply because we have received a letter or something of that kind from the railway officials. Everything that could be done by the Government to ascertain the facts in connection with these extensions was done. It was shown that settlement in these districts was ahead of the railways and that the extensions should be built. As to the roads being profitable, we have the statement of the officials. There is no doubt about their being profitable. They will run intoi a splendid section of the country, where the settlers will furnish a sufficient quantity of traffic in farm products to make them pay. My candid opinion is that extensions such as this, which produce more traffic for our main lines and promote settlement, will help reduce the deficits on the Canadian National railways. We have been informed by the officials that owing to the high cost of rails and labour the roads will cost from $30,000 to $35,000 a mile. Of course, we shall have more traffic the second year than the first, because settlement will proceed much more rapidly when the railway accommodation is provided.
Does the minister mean to say that he has no written report at all from some responsible officer with regard to these extensions?

We have a statement from the president, after the discussions we had. There is an official report as to the necessity of the extensions we are asking for and the conditions of the country through which they will run. I do not want the committee to think I am trying to rush this Bill through in an unreasonable manner. There will be another opportunity to discuss these extensions when the Estimates are up, and if the committee want a report on each extension I will have the reports brought down. I am trying to get this legislation through because I think, and the Government thinks, that these extensions are absolutely necessary.

This country is divided into two camps as far as public ownership is concerned. On the one side we have the people of this country and the Government, and on the other the Canadian Pacific. Now we, the representatives of the people, sitting here, have the same responsibilities as the directors and managers of the Canadian Pacific would have if they were projecting new lines, and I venture to tell my hon. friend that the president and the executive of the Canadian Pacific would not plunge into the building of a road into practically uninhabited sections of the West without a report from a responsible engineer as to the feasibility of building the road, and a report from the traffic manager as to the prospects of the road paying. All that is done in this case is that the Minister of Railways goes on a little excursion to Toronto and while there he has the pleasure of sitting down and smoking a cigar with Mr. Hanna and Mr. MacLeod
I do not smoke.
He takes his whiskey while they smoke.
There is prohibition in Ontario.

We have no report, no plan, no estimate. We are not told whether bridges will have to be built to cross [DOT]streams, whether there are any rock cuttings to be made, or anything as to the nature of the road. All we have is this solemn gathering of two or three friends discussing matters generally and reaching the conclusion that it would be a nice thing to extend lines in certain parts of the country. Then the minister comes home and calls this easy bunch of members around him and asks them to give him any quantity of money to build this road. I submit to the minister and to this House that that is not the way to do business. Before one dollar is voted for this proposition and before a charter is granted we should ascertain the facts in a business-like way. I am not talking from an opposition standpoint or with any idea of blocking this project. I am only asking that the proper line of business be-followed, as I understand it, and which hon. gentlemen opposite who are business men would follow if they were investing their own money. We are the trustees of the money of the people. The people are losing by the National railways something like $49,000,000 or $50,000,000 a year, and now we are telling the people of

this country that notwithstanding the fact that we, the trustees of their money, lost something like $50,000,000 on the railways last year, we .are going to continue to spend money on the railways without consulting them, and with no hope of doing better in the future than in the past. If that is the way we are going to wield our power under the policy of Government ownership, the enemies of public ownership and those who criticise it, of whom I am one, will have a splendid opportunity of finding themselves justified by the facts. Has the minister any working profile of these extensions showing the number of bridges and cuttings and so forth, and also an estimate of the probable expenditure involved? Has an Order in Council been passed approving the location of the different lines? All this information would be given if it was any one but ourselves who was building these roads. We are simply dealing with ourselves unde' the name of this company. It is somewhat of a fallacious position to be in. We are calling ourselves the Canadian Northern Railway, whereas it is ourselves who are building these roads. We have all the powers under the Railway Act to enable us to build a railway, and in view of that Act on the statute books it is anomalous that we should be here asking power of ourselves to build our own road, and talking of the road as if it was .anybody else's but our own. I think I have made myself perfectly clear, and I am sure my argument must appeal to every business man in this House. I think the committee should be given the information I have asked for I am not a business man myself; 'I am a mere lawyer, but whatever may be said of lawyers, after they have been a long time in practice they learn something about business. I have learned business ideas. I think it is only plain common sense that we should be given the information I have asked for before we are asked to launch upon this very doubtful enterprise.

I think if my hon. friend took a trip out West and saw conditions for himself he would change his mind as to the necessity of building these roads. I wish to say a word in regard to subclause (a), as the line mentioned therein is in the constituency I represent. The country lying to the north of Prince Albert is thickly settled for the reason that when settlers went in there the odd number homesteads were open for entry the .same as the even numbers, which was very different from what it had been in former years. We therefore have more
settlers to the square mile there than in the greater part of the West. For some twenty-five or thirty miles this thick settlement continues north of Prince Albert, and the settlers have been in that country for a good many years, some for a very long period. They have been looking forward to railway facilities but up to the present time they have not been able to secure anything. Beyond that, twenty-five or thirty miles, you still find men growing wheat and raising cattle, and their produce has to be transported in many instances thirty and even forty miles. At Prince Albert we have just recently had provincial stock yards opened and they are promising to be very successful, and there is a large abattoir operating at the same point. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) mentioned the difficulty of getting wheat out of the northern district last year, and I can vouch for what he says in that respect. I would point out that on general principles it is necessary to build these branch lines, because if you want to make the railroad pay it is essential to open up just such a district as this line will go into. I therefore most heartily endorse the principle laid down here.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: It might be interesting to the committee to know who owns the land along this particular section. In am not particularly interested in regard to what is owned by settlers who have located, but it would be interesting to know what companies own big tracts of this country in which the railway is to operate, and how much the Crown owns.

I will endeavour to have that information when my Estimates are under consideration. I believe that that particular section from Prince Albert north was Government land that has been settled by soldiers. There is a large settlement of returned soldiers in that particular locality. The other districts, I understand, are nearly all settled by private settlers. However, I will get the information which my hon. friend desires. I have not heard of any large company owning any land there. So far as I am aware it is owned by private settlers interested in the locality.

I think the minister will have to revise his figures in regard to the population. I may remind him that the last census taken in Saskatchewan only four years ago showed that there were only 42,000 people in the whole district, and the population of the southern

part of Prince Albert district must be subtracted from that number in order to give the true population of the northern part of the country. I think that -the minister must be misinformed in regard to the number of people who will be served by the new branches in that territory, and if he could get the exact information for us it might be useful. I believe he could obtain that information because a census was taken there a few years ago.

An hon. member asked me if I knew what the population was and I replied that I could not make any authoritative statement myself, but I thought it had been mentioned in the committee. I think that an hon. member sitting behind me said it was 40,000. If I remember rightly it was the hon. member who lives in Prince Albert that made that statement. This railway, of course, would not. serve the whole of that 40,000, but it would serve a large proportion of them. I did not make the statement on my own responsibility.

It was I who said that the population of the constituency was forty thousand. It may be considerably more dhan that at the present time. As to this particular district, it would be difficult to estimate what the difference is, because the settlers have been going there continuously for some years, and since the establishment of the Soldiers' Settlement Board there has been a large influx into the northern part of this district. The soldiers have settled very extensively there, and it would be difficult to state the exact population.

speechtext:
The hon. member and his supporters voted for the proposition that the coal used for the Canadian railways carrying freight shall be taken out on the basis of nine hours pay for eight hours'

work. Is it the intention to build these railways on the same basis?

The railways will be
built under contract. Tenders will be called, and the contractor will have to arrange with those whom he may employ to construct the railways. I cannot say whether he will employ them for nine hours or ten hours.

We are evidently dealing with Mackenzie and Mann because they are synonymous with the Canadian Northern and being synonymous with the Canadian Northern they are going to build this road. Our experience is that Mackenzie and Mann, as railway operators, always lost money and that to make up the vacum in their purses they used to come to the Government of Canada. While they always lost money as operators they always made money as contractors. Mackenzie and Mann made themselves millionaires by building roads for themselves. That ridiculous anomaly has existed in this country for the last twenty-five or forty years. I would like to ask if Mackenzie and Mann are going to be permitted to make a contract with the Mackenzie and Mann Construction Company for the building of these roads in order that they may make millions for themselves and if when they come to run the roads they will run into the treasury of this country.

I can hardly think that my hon. friend is fair in the manner in which he puts the matter. He states that this road is really the property of Mackenzie and Mann. It is now the road of the people of Canada.
Why do you use their names?

I explained a minute ago
that any construction that has to be done for subsidiary companies must be done under the name of the parent company. But even if we continue the name the hon. member must admit that this is government property and not the property of Mackenzie and Mann. The management call for tenders for each particular piece of road that is to be built and a number of people tender. The lowest tender is accepted in every case. I do not think that there is any fairer way of doing it or that it could be done in any other way. It is not Mackenzie and Mann at all. The hon. gentleman states that Mackenzie and Mann made millions out of the Canadian Northern. I hardly agree with him. I do not think that Mackenzie and Mann are the millionaires the hon. gentleman states them to be. However that has nothing to do with the matter; the board of management call for tenders, the lowest tenderer will be given the contract and it will be carried out under the supervision of the railway employees who are in no way connected with Mackenzie and Mann.

Last year we put
through a Bill consolidating all the Government railways to which the Bill was attached a schedule containing the names of twenty or thirty different roads that were to be built afterwards.
Forty.

Some one says forty; it was a large number anyway. Will the minister tell us how many of these different branches have been built since and if any of the branches mentioned m this Bill are identical with any of those mentioned in the schedule to the Bill which was passed a session or two ago.

Yes; these charters are parts of the subsidiary companies. In Saskatchewan there was the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan Railway Company and in Alberta the Canadian Northern Alberta, both subsidiary to the Canadian Northern railway. These are extensions of the lines that were built under those charters. They will be a part of the several hundred miles of railway already built. The Canadian Northern Railway system has about 9,000 miles of which there, are probably 1,090 miles in Eastern Canada and in British Columbia and about 7,000 in the western provinces. This in each case adds about fifty miles to the lines that were mentioned in the schedule to the Bill which was passed by Parliament.

Those who are familiar with the geography of the country will have no difficulty in forming an impression cf the extent of the obligation we are assuming, but after all there are only a few who are so blessed as to have that knowledge. It would be a convenience to have some indication of the mileage expressed in this Bill. My recollection is that in all our railway Bills the mileage is mentioned. There may be cases in which you cannot be precise. My recollection is that in all our railway appropriations we would indicate the mileage at so many miles, more or less. That is convenient to put in your Bill. Here you do not say whether you are going to build a thousand miles or twenty. I suggest

that until the minister has had a careful calculation made he would be proceeding on a safe basis to indicate the probable mileage of the road in order to help anybody who reads the Bill on a future occasion.

It was stated in the committee by me, as well as by the railway officials, in each case, that the distance would not exceed fifty miles. I have no objection, if the committee wishes it, to carrying out the suggestion of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's and adding in each clause, "Not exceeding fifty miles".

I would not put in the words, "not exceeding", because the points are designated, but I would say so many miles more or less. I do not want to restrict my hon. friend at all, but if somebody- who is not familiar with the country-reads the Bill in future he ought to be given some idea as to the mileage in each case.

Might I point out
another emendation to this legislation which would help the ordinary reader in time to come? The Bill is entitled, "An Act respecting the Canadian National Railways", and it is stated that it may be referred to as "The Canadian National Railways Act 1920". Then the Bill proceeds to refer to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. The sooner the minister, who is responsible for the railway administration and policy of this country, will put the different roads which form part of the National Railways System into the possession of the National Railway Company and call them by their proper' names, just so soon will he confer a real benefit on any one who wants to study our railway situation now and in the future. It is not really a question of names, it is a question of being able to understand the situation thoroughly; and this habit of calling systems of railway, or branch lines of railway, which properly belong to the National system, by their former names breeds confusion, and makes it less possible to understand the railway situation which exists at the present time.
If I understand the hon. member he wishes to eliminate the name, "Canadian Northern Railway" and adopt the title of "Canadian National Railway"?

I understood from the minister at an earlier part of the discussion that this part of the system now referred to has not yet been vested in the Canadian National system, and that was the reason why the name, "Canadian National Rail-
	j .	,
way", was not employed. If this system itself now falls under our National system I see no reason why the name should not be changed by the committee now.

I explained a few
minutes ago that in the case of the Canadian Northern or of these extensions of a subsidiary company even when the Canadian Northern stock is transferred to the Canadian National Company those extensions Rave to be asked for in the name of the Canadian Northern, or the subsidiary company. I have been in the railway committee for a good many years, and during that time-and even as late as the present session-whenever the Canadian Railway Company applied for an extension of its charter they did so in the name of the subsidiary company, although they would do away with that plan if they could. I am informed by the legal authorities of the railway that this is the proper plan to pursue-that the name of the company or the subsidiary must be employed.

I can understand that as the law now stands the minister's position is right when it is a case of continuing charters possessed by subsidiary companies and operating under them. But that difficulty could be overcome and the point raised by the hon. member for Brome could be met by legislation-passed either at this or another session-transferring all the powers of these various companies to the Canadian National Railway Company. After that there would be no need of continuing the name "Canadian Northern". It would be a proper thing to do and we should not have the confusion which results from using the terms "Canadian National" and "Canadian Northern" which confusion is all the greater because the initials are the same in both cases.

Before the clause carries I
desire to say that this discussion would not have been so long drawn out had it not been for the unfair action taken by hon. gentlemen opposite in refusing to allow members on this side to discuss this measure, and the matters connected with it, as freely as they have taken the opportunity of doing themselves. The character of this Bill is such as to encourage members in other sections of Canada in need of branch lines, or extensions, to ask why they should not be granted the same privilege. When that line of argument was followed, the Chairman ruled it was out of order, and he asked the House to give unanimous consent in order that the discussion might be

continued. Hon. gentlemen opposite, however refused to give that consent, and thus restricted the scope of the debate as regards members on this side. Hon. gentlemen opposite did that despite the fact that every session the Opposition agree to deviations from the rules-when the session is well advanced-in order to expedite business.
The Minister of Railways is asking permission to build lines of railway along the following routes:
A line from a point at or near Prince Albert thence northerly to a point at or near township fifty-seven, range twenty-live, west of the second meridian, with a branch line commencing at a point on above line at or near township fifty-two, range twenty-five, west of the second meridian, and running in a generally easterly direction to range fifteen west of the second meridian;

The paragraph stops there.

I read two or three more lines than I need have read. But in reference to the line of railway my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) ,i.s asking this committee to grant a charter .for. I think he said a few moments ago, in answer to an inquiry by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fieilding), that it would be something like 50 miles in length, and I also understood him to say that the estimated cost of construction would be about $35,000 per mile. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that that is not sufficient information. I think, the hon. minister, as representing the Canadian Northern railway, which is asking for this charter, should be in a position to give this committee information regarding the territory through which this railway will run, the population in the settlements along the route, and the traffic possibilities, so that hon. members will be able to decide whether or not it be in the interests of the Canadian National system to grant this charter. This
line is going to cost a large amount of money to build, and, as has been pointed out, other portions of the Canadian National Railway system have cost this country a great deal of money. The question that naturally arises in the minds of every hon. member is: Whether this construction is going to 'be in the interests of Canada and of the system as a whole, and of public ownership? Some information, I submit, should be given by the Minister of Railways before he asks this committee to accept his proposition.
I take the next branch line:
From a point on the main line of the Canadian National railways between the crossing of the North Saskatchewan River and Radis-son, thence in a generally northerly and northwesterly direction to a point on the Company's authorized line at or near Meeting Lake;
What is required in regard to the railway suggested in section (a) is also required in regard to this railway: we should have accurate information. It is all very well for the Minister of Railways to say: "We have all this information in the vaults of the Canadian National railway in the city of Toronto." But what good is that to hon. members? The information should be brought before this committee. It is of no interest to hon. members to know that Mr. Hanna says that this is going to be a paying proposition, nor is it of any interest to me, Sir, to be told that the Board of Directors of the Canadian National railways believe this will be a paying proposition. If they have that information available, it should be here, not in the city of Toronto.

I would like to ask the hon. member if he does not know in regard to that particular section of railway that the information given to the Railway Committee on the points he mentions convinced every member of that committee from his side of the House of the potential value of the road and they wanted to give the route to their particular friends, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company?

Loud and prolonged applause ! I may tell my hon. friend that I. know nothing about what, took place in the Railway Committee-and a great many hon. members on this side of the House are in the same position. If that information was brought before the Railway Committee, then, Sir, I say that is all the greater reason why it should be brought before this committee. And if that information was before the Railway Committee it surely would
The points where the roads start.
How far?

I cannot give that information now; I do not happen to have it before me. Of course, the hon. member is entitled to all information in connection with the matter, and I wall not ask that the Bill go through if hon. members do not want it to go through without this information being furnished. But these Railway Bills are sent to the Railway Committee so that all this detailed information may be submitted to and considered by that committee. That procedure was followed in this case; the railway officials appeared before the committee; the information was obtained, and the committee unanimously passed the Bill. If the hon. member wants all these files and details I have no objection to getting the information for him; no hon. member will be able to say that I withheld information. If it is his intention to hold up the Bill in the absence of this information, of course, I must submit. But the fact that the money must subsequently he voted for this purpose would seem to justify the passing of the Bill, particularly in view of the fact that all the details were considered by the Railway Committee.
Mr. 'COPP: My hon. friend should not suggest that it is my purpose to hold up the Bill. I have only occupied about ten or fifteen minutes of the time of the committee; the minister has taken an hour or two in discussing his side of it. It is not my intention unnecessarily to delay the Bill, but I do think we should have more direct and accurate information in regard to it. If the information was before the Railway Committee, surely it would' not take long to place it before this committee.

At Six o'clock the committee took recess.
