speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have
listened with a great deal of interest to what the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) had to say in regard to the proposed Bill. This Bill is the product of the very best experts of the department of Agriculture who have carefully consulted the stock men, mill men and every one else whom we knew of as taking an interest in the feed business. There are about 150,000 tons of screenings at the head of the Lakes each year as a result of the cleaning process carried on in the elevators at that point. For several years feeds for livestock have been extremely scarce. Our American friends, being keenly alive to the value of these feeding stuffs, have been

very glad to import them into the United States. Rut on account of the scarcity of feed on this side, we deemed it advisable to utilize every possible pound of feed for caring for our stock. In actual experiments, as was mentioned by the hon. member for South Oxford, it has been proven that screenings are often better than bran in nutritive quality. I consider that we would not be doing our duty in sending these screenings out of the country or destroying them.
The objects of this particular Bill are to so guard against noxious weeds and to place these feeds before the public in such a condition that the farmer may know exactly what he is getting and so may be able to buy something that he knows all about. Heretofore these feeds have been adulterated to a very great extent, they have been sold and advertised very freely, and in many cases the farmer did not obtain what he thought he was getting. He paid a high price for feed which was in many cases very poor in quality, consisting of a mixture of oat hulls, ground straw, etc. By this Bill we propose to guard against that as far as possible.
My hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) wanted to know why we do not keep out these seeds altogether. I may say that it is impossible, with the machinery which we have at our disposal at the present time, to entirely remove all seeds. In the case of bran, if the bran is turned out pure, consisting of the product of the wheat grain, with the small amount of seed that it is impossible to remove, it may be sold for bran, but the moment weed seeds are added to the bran it comes under the heading of commercial feeding stuffs and under the control of our inspectors.
In regard to black seed occurring in these screenings, I may say that our experiments have shown that as feeding stuffs it has almost no value at all, in addition to which it has been proven poisonous to small pigs. Under the regulations which it is proposed to make in connection with this Bill, we will control the actual amount of these black seeds, so that when the farmer buys a bag of commercial feeding stuffs he will have clearly stated on a tag the percentage of different grains contained therein and also the percentage of weed seeds. He will therefore buy it with his eyes entirely open and be able to judge for himself. It it very wide of the mark to say that the sale of screenings in this country has had any effect whatever on the reduction of our dairy products. We all know that owing to high wages and also to the high cost of

feed, the man who keeps an inferior cow on his place finds it utterly impossible to pay these prices and carry on dairying at a profit.
However, there are other men who maintain herds of higher quality who are making dairying pay well under present conditions. As far as prices are concerned I cannot clearly understand how the hon. member for South Oxford can possibly expect to buy cheap bran and cheap shorts produced from wheat that is ranging in price around $3 a bushel.

I am sure the minister would not misquote what ! stated. I do not think I made any reference to the price. It was pure bran, not cheap bran, that I was advocating, I realize that the price of the commodity must be regulated by the price of the grain, and by supply and demand.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I may have been mistaken but I thought what the hon. member stated was that it was owing to the quality of this feed that dairy men were almost afraid to feed it to their cows-
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: and that therefore our dairy production U'as much less than it should be.
Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I think the hon. member will find that the falling off in dairy produce has been due rather to the lack of feed than to the quality of it.
With regard to this board which the minister is empowered to call under the proposed Act, I may say that it will probably be composed of one milling man, two of three livestock men probably, two or three men from the Department of Agriculture, and perhaps one dealer in feed, so that each section of the business will be fully represented. We are calling in their assistance so that we will arrive at a proper set of regulations that will be practicable and will work out well in all directions.
While the hon. member for South Oxford takes a rather pessimistic view of the present livestock conditions in this country, his brother farmers in Ontario apparently do not feel that way. It was only yesterday that I, along with the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie), had the pleasure of speaking at a picnic at Guelph where we celebrated the purchase in the Old Country of a bull for which 534,000 was paid,

the highest price ever paid in the British Empire tor a bull. Then, last week, two more Holstein breeders of Ontario went down to Minneapolis and purchased a two months' old calf for ?50,000. Apparently, therefore, all the farmers in Ontario do not feel pessimistic regarding the future of the livestock business. Now, Mr. Speaker, as I have already said, this Bill has been carefully prepared. No doubt it is not perfect, it is quite likely that some improvements can be made in it, but it has been given very careful consideration by a set of experts in the Department of Agriculture who have carefully consulted many of the livestock men, and they think it is just about as perfect as it can be made under present conditions. Certainly it is an improvement on any of the legislation which has been enacted in the past. It will insure purer feed and will enable the farmer to know exactly what he is getting when he buys feed for his stock.
I would like to know what provision has been made in the present Bill with regard to the use of bran and shorts for feed.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Under this Bill as long
as a man sells bran and shorts in a pure state, or as nearly pure as is possible, he is permitted to do so, but the moment he adds any weeds not in compliance with the regulations it' becomes "commercial feeding stuff'' instead of bran, and he can be prosecuted.
I should add, in addition to what I have already stated, that this Bill was given very careful consideration by the Committee of Agriculture of the House, and was adopted by it unanimously.
Motion for the second reading of the Bill agreed to, and the House went into committee, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section >2-definition:

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
I suppose the minister understands that the term, "entire clean grain" would mean grain as delivered by the farmer to the mill. But supposing there was some pigeon grass in it?
Mr. TOLMIE,:	If it did not contain too
large a proportion of poisonous weed seeds it would then be suitable for chop feed; but if it contained a large quantity of those it would come under the head of "com-merciaU feeding stuff."

I see that under
paragraph 1 of this section commercial feeding stuffs is defined as meaning "any
article offered for sale for the feeding of livestock and poultry." Under paragraph (d) it is held not to include bran, shorts or middlings when unmixed with other materials. Then subclause 3 contains this definition:
"feeding stuff" means any commercial feeding stuff, bran, shorts or middlings and chop feed.
Then I notice that in the balance of the Bill " feeding stuff " is referred to instead of " commercial feeding stuff " when one would almost infer that commercial feeding stuff was intended, and that bran and ' shorts would be referred to as feeding stuff. What is the object of these variations? What is the meaning of having bran and shorts when unmixed with other materials defined as commercial feeding stuffs? Is it contemplated that bran and shorts are to be mixed by the mixers of feed, and that only whenever they see fit bran and shorts are to be sold as bran and shorts? I am satisfied that is about the effect of it, because if people cannot buy the bran and shorts they will certainly have to do the next best thing, and buy a mixture containing, maybe, a very large proportion of bran- and shorts, and some other materials that have been added. It is absolutely impossible to carry on without having mill feeds of this kind. What is the effect of the two terms used?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Just as long as bran and shorts are named bran and shorts they are sold as such. If they are mixed with any of these seeds or other feeds, then they are classified under " commercial feeding stuffs." The term " feeding stuffs " in this Bill applies to all of those feeds.
Even to " commercial feeding stuffs"?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes.
Consequently there is in the following section no distinction between mixtures of this kind and pure bran and shorts, because you say the term "feeding stuff" covers both.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Pure bran and shorts
under section 6 will -be sold as bran and shorts; but immediately they are mixed, as I have already pointed out, they are considered to be "commercial feeding stuffs."

The effect of this
clause will be that mill feeds of this kind will be mixed, and you will get but a very small proportion of pure bran and shorts. This clause is a departure from the old

Act, and instead of being an advance along the lines which we desire it is going in the opposite direction. It is making provision for the mixing of all these feeding stuffs and having the mixture disposed of to suit the convenience of the mill feed men.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: On the contrary, Mr. Chairman, there are no restrictions at all on pure bran and shorts, so there is every encouragement for a man to sell them as bran and shorts; but the moment he mixes them with other grains the mixture is classed as a commercial feeding stuff and has to be so described on the label.

I do not notice .any strong desire on the part of the millers or anybody to-day to sell pure bran and shorts; it is absolutely impossible to find them offered for sale. Safeguards to insure their purity should be provided. That is why I take objection to this Bill, in that it does not provide the safeguards which are necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Those who sell bran and shorts nowadays are certainly encouraged to mix other ingredients, because there is no such legislation as this, in force. That is why they mix cheaper feed with bran and shorts. The aim of this Bill is to insure that the farmer shall know what he is buying and shall get what he pays for.

In this clause the minister does
not define what is meant by "bran, shorts and middlings." We who are feeding these feeds to our stocks every day have good reason to suspect that what we buy as bran, shorts and middlings are not of th^ quality they used to be. Would it not be possible to define bran, shorts and middlings in such a way as to prohibit the mixing of weed seeds or anything of that kind with them? Perhaps I am reading the Bill wrongly, but I fail to see anything in it that covers this point. I quite understand that immediately weed seeds or similar ingredients are mixed with bran and shorts the mixture becomes a "feeding stuff," and of course comes under the jurisdiction of the inspectors of the department. But even that might not attain the end sought. I think it would be better to prohibit the mixing of anything at all with bran and shorts, because we look upon these articles as being standard and something we can rely on.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
I was going to suggest that the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) is absolutely right in his view of how the legislation may work out, pro-

viding conditions are continued as they have existed in this country since 1917. If the hon. gentleman will a little later on in the session support the continuation of the Wheat Board, giving it power to fix the price of bran and shorts away down below the market price of the world, he will have the same experience again as he had in the past; there will be a scarcity of bran and shorts. No legislation will make bran and shorts more plentiful in this country; that, is the whole secret-and I am speaking from experience as a man in the milling . business. The only way to get a plentiful supply of pure bran and shorts is to leave the trade to regulate itself and sell these articles at the prevailing market price of the world. Under such conditions we in Canada would not have to pay more than bran and shorts are worth anywhere else. But if we attempt by legislation to fix the price at $10 or $15 a ton below what pure bran and shorts are really worth, and, on the other hand, enable the same board to place a tax of $1.50 to1 $2 a barrel on flour to distribute among the men who have grown the wheat from which that flour was produced, we are going to have in this country a continuation of the same experience that my hon. friend has been complaining of for the last hour and a half-a scarcity of mill feed.

I do not know that the matter referred to by the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) has much to do with the subject matter of this clause. As far as I am personally concerned I am not in favour of fixing the prices of anything; I (believe the law of supply and demand should govern, and if mill feeds are worth a certain price, that price should be paid rather than an arbitrary price fixed by the Government. But I want to refer again to the phrase "commercial feeding stuffs" which is defined in this clause. The clause continues;
"'commercial feeding stuffs" does not include bran, shorts or middlings, when unmixed with other materials.
Then subsection 3 says:
"feeding stuff' means any commercial feeding stuff, bran, shorts or middlings and chop feed.
To my mind those two provisions are absolutely contradictory, I fail to understand what object is desired to be attained by these contradictory provisions. I think that the suggestion of the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy) is a very good one, and that we should define what constitutes bran and shorts. We are em-

powering the minister by regulation to do a whole lot of things, and we are somewhat mystified by the definitions contained in this Bill, which, as I have pointed out, are apparently absolutely contradictory.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think the Bill is quite clear, Mr. Chairman. "Feeding stuffs" in the working out of this Bill is a general term applied to all feeding stuffs dealt with herein. In regard to the definition covering bran and shorts, I may say that it will be necessary in the regulations to distinguish several feeds, not only bran and shorts, but also cotton seed cake, oil meal, fish meal, oat hulls, and many of those other ingredients that are used in the manufacture of feeding stuffs It is better to have that matter controlled by regulation, for the reason that from time to time a certain amount of elasticity may be necessary to meet prevailing conditions. For instance, during the war flour extraction from wheat was increased 5 or 6 per cent, and this was done at the expense of bran, so that bran before the war was quite a different article from that which was produced under the new wheat regulations.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-labels on commercial feeding stuffs:

Subsection (2) provides:
In the case of car lots in bulk, the provisions of this section shall be held to be complied with if the statement required by this section is attached to the invoice or bill of lading delivered to the purchaser.
The feeder who goes to buy from the dealer at the car may not have access to that statement, which is in the possession of the dealer. Will the minister insert a provision there to the effect that the state-*ment required by this section must be made available to the purchaser in such a case?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: A dealer who buys such material in bulk and who retails it in sacks must attach to each sack a tag upon which is clearly shown what the contents of the bag are.

When the dealer gets a carload of material in bulk the farmer usually goes to the car with his own sacks, and the material is bagged and sold directly out of the car. I doubt whether the dealer would be willing to attach a tag to every sack put up in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
He violates the provisions of the Act if he does not. If the purchaser
is not certain as to the actual content he may secure a pound of the material and send it to our analyst at Ottawa. A careful analysis of the feed will be made and if it is not in accordance with what it is represented to be, prosecution will follow.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-registration:

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Why is not the registration period made to run concurrently with the fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It was considered that the arrangement as set forth in the section would be most convenient to the trade.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-use of injurious ingredients prohibited:

In this clause we should be a little more definite; there should be -some statement as to what the regulations are to be. The committee are surely entitled to know what the views of the minister .are in respect to the quantity of weed seeds, damaged grain, and so on, which may be used as a constituent of any feeding stuffs.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In the merchandising of re-cleaned screenings, the standard sample which formed the basis for contract delivery contained less than one per cent by weight of "black seeds" that are capable of passing through a screen with perforations one-fourteenth inch in diameter. These "black seeds" are not all harmful, but contain practically all of the weed seeds
10 p.m. that are injurious to the health of stock. It is better to handle this matter by regulation, owing to the changed conditions which prevail from time to time. In some years more of these screenings are contained in the grain than in others. Certain varieties of seeds are not as large in some dry seasons as they are in ordinary seasons. In the making of these regulations, producers, millers, consumers and experts of the department will be consulted, so that information will be secured from every possible angle. It is not the aim of the department to make regulations that we shall not be able to carry out or which will not be beneficial. By consultation with these different interests it is contemplated that the regulations made will be applicable to the conditions and will render good service.

I appreciate the fact that a sieve with a certain kind of mesh

will take out the most objectionable seeds, but I can hardly appreciate the force of the argument that the variability of the seasons would affect the size of the seeds. I think that the size of the seeds varies very little indeed. I am still of the opinion that we should incorporate in the Bill such provisions as the minister intends to embody in these regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not think that nearly as good service could be rendered in that way. It is better to enable the making of regulations to fit the situation from one year to another.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 8-to .be free from weed seeds:
Mr. SUTHERLAND; Here again this matter is to be dealt with by regulations that we know nothing about. We must take it for granted that some experts somewhere who know all about this are going to embody in the regulations legislation for the people of Canada. As far as I am concerned, I do not consider that that is why I have been sent here. If there is such wisdom in the minds of these people, I think the minister ought to submit it to the House in concrete form, raither than to ask us to empower him to deal with this matter by regulations that we are not acquainted with to-day. It is proposed to let the clause pass without any explanation. In view of the fact that so many clauses of this Bill empower the minister to deal wih these matters by regulation, in view also of the fact that the minister has entirely ignored the statement I made on the second reading of the Bill, and that he stated that ample provision would be made for safeguarding the purity of these mill feeds and that the Act of last session was still on the statute book, which Act I have shown clearly and conclusively was repealed by the Bill introduced by the Minister of Health, and further, as there is no provision in this Bill to ensure the purity of bran and shorts, I think it would ibe advisable to strike out this clause entirely which permits the minister to deal with the matter by regulation after consulting with very wise people in the East and in the West it may be. In view of these considerations and the fact that no explanation has been made by the minister I beg to move, seconded by the bon. member for Muakoka (Mr. McGibbon:)
That clause 8 as printed in the Bill be struck therefrom and the following- substituted therefor :	[DOT]
"In the case of bran, shorts or middlings, it shall be considered to be adulterated if it con-

tains anything- that is not a product of wheat, or, in the case of corn bran, if it contains anything- that is not a product of maize or Indian corn."
This Bill is far from complete, and we shall be much worse off than at any time in the past if it goes through in its present form. I am therefore moving that the provision passed at the last session be embodied in the Bill, instead of empowering the minister to consult somebody who will by some process of reasoning embody something in the regulations that we do not know anything at all about.

I am of the impression that the definition of bran and shorts should come under section 6, where provision is made for dealing with bran and shorts. I do not think the definition should be inserted in section 8.
Amendment negatived.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-certificate of analysis as evidence:
Who pays the cost of analysis of samples?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It is free so far as the
working of this Bill is concerned.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 12-analysis, etc., may be published:

What is hoped to
be accomplished by this section, and why is the word "may" used instead of saying that the minister "shall" publish?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It was thought better to leave it to the discretion of the minister whether to publish the results or not. Take the case oif a large dealer who can stand a fine of $200, or $300 or $400 without feeling very much injured. If it is published throughout the country that he is selling feed that has been adulterated, he would suffer to a much greater extent than by the fine. That is why it is .left to the discretion of the minister.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 14-regulations:

We all appreciate
the fact that instead of using the employees now available in the various branches of the Government, the Civil Service is being added to continually. I understand from the remarks the minister made the other night that he does not contemplate appoint-

ing a permanent board, but merely a board with whom he can consult from time to time with reference to this matter. I again wish to repeat that I am disappointed that Parliament is being absolutely ignored in this matter of regulations. The minister asks Parliament to let him consult with and act upon the advice of men whom he says will know much better than the people who will be held responsible for this legislation by the people of this country. As far as I am concerned, I am absolutely opposed to such a procedure. I object to the passing of this section.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.
I ask that the yeas and nays be counted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Tolmie moves that clause 14 stand as part of the Bill. Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt the motion?
Some hon. MEMBERS : Yes.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In my opinion the
yeas have it. I declare the section agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 17

innocent purchaser protected :

In regard to the question of costs I think an extraordinary principle is introduced here. This is a criminal offense, and while it is not very serious, nevertheless it must be dealt with as a criminal offense, and the principles of criminal law must be applied. The question in a criminal action is whether a man is guilty or not. If he is guilty he should be punished, and if he is found not guilty, whatever may have happened is by that very fact proved to have been due to no fault of his. He is declared not guilty and is therefore entirely innocent of any offense, and there can be no reason whatever why he should be mulched in costs. The provision of this Bill is a new doctrine to me and, I have no doubt, to every lawyer in the House. If a man is not guilty he should not be subject to any penalty, and the costs in a criminal proceeding are part of the penalty. In this clause you provide that although a man may prove himself absolutely innocent, although he may know that he had no knowledge that there was anything wrong in the transaction, did not know that there was any deleterious substance in the stuff, and considered that everything
was all right, being confident that he was not violating the law; and although the court may have found him not guilty, nevertheless he shall " be liable upon conviction for the costs of the prosecution only." I do not know what advice the minister has received on the point, iflit it seems to me to be a new departure in criminal law procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is not an entirely new ' departure, for it has been a part of the Seed Control Act for the last fifteen years and it has been found to work very smoothly. All that is necessary is to ask the retailer to go before a justice of the peace and make a sworn statement which will cost from fifty cents to a dollar, and this is essential before we can begin prosecution of the manufacturer who sold the goods.

There is another peculiar feature about this section. The magistrate can, without a hearing, pronounce judgment upon the information laid before him. Surely that is an extraordinary line of procedure. Before a man can be pronounced innocent or otherwise evidence must be taken and the person who lays the charge must be called upon to substantiate it. But as I understand the situation, some one can go before the magistrate and make an affidavit and without a hearing of the other side, the case is decided. That seems to be another new departure.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have no legal training, and I can only say that this provision has v been working very smoothly for fifteen years in the Seed Control Act, from which it was taken.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Rt. Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) Bill No. 138 to amend the Penitentiary Act was read a second time and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Minister to have power to make regulations for administration, etc., of penitentiaries:
Is it proposed that the minister himself shall make these regulations without the assent of Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the law the administration is, by the clause to which these words are to be added, placed in the hands
34i0
^o penalties attached?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No penalties attached.
Was there not a commission appointed to investigate the treatment of the prisoners in the various penitentiaries, and was there not a report made to the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have not had any recent investigation.

speakerposition: stagedirection

Section agreed to.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Rt. Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) Bill No. 137, to amend the Criminal Code was read a second time and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Definitions of appeal court amended to meet changes in title of courts:
Did the minister, on the first reading,, explain the general purpose of this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, in so far as there is a general principle, but as there are amendments to different articles of the code it can hardly be said that there is any principle running through the Bill. The first section is for the purpose of making the names of courts conform to the changes which have been made in the names of those courts by provincial legislation.
For the purpose of naming the appeal courts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In regard to the first paragraph, there is no change, and the reason they came to be included was that we desired to include all the provisions about the courts. With reference to the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and British Columbia the Code says that the appeal court shall be the "supreme court en banc." In New Brunswick and in British Columbia the legislatures have altered the constitution of their courts and instead of having one court with an appeal to that court sitting en banc, they have constituted a court of appeal and a court of first instance. In order to have these 
proceedings, which are proceedings intended to go to the court of appeal, go to the court of appeal of the province, we have to make this modification. There is no longer a court that sits en banc to hear appeals. This is simply to meet the change in the constitution of the provincial courts as brought about by provincial legislation.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-permit required for firearms and certain weapons:
Wherein does this provision differ from the existing law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It differs by extending
the provisions so as to make it cover all classes.
Additional weapons?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All firearms. Heretofore it was limited to arms that could be concealed upon the person. The Criminal Code was amended last year, and in order to show the precise difference I must refer to the Statutes of 1919.
Never mind doing that, the general purpose can be stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the purpose.

A British subject is
only relieved from the necessity of obtaining a license in respect to any shot gun which he owns, but if such a person were to buy a shot gun the license provision applies. If a man now has a shot gun he is all right; but if his neighbour thinks it proper to purchase a shot gun in order to shoot partridge, duck or the like, he must obtain a license. That is making a discrimination of which I do not quite see the force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I may say it was considered desirable under existing -conditions that we should have a control over the trade in firearms generally. Reports coming from the police, and coming also to some extent from information reaching the military authorities, indicated that in certain localities at different periods there was what looked like an extraordinary movement in the acquisition of firearms. It was thought desirable that we should have a control over them, and therefore we have the system established which existed previously in the case of a certain class of firearms, and which existed previously as regards aliens. Now it is extended so as to cover the acquisition and possession of firearms generally. It did not seem right, however, that a British subject-who under the law as it stood was under no restriction as

regards this class of arms-should be controlled as regards those arms that he had already acquired. This is in order to make the law operative-in so far as it imposes any restriction in regard to shot guns-only with respect to the future. That is the purpose of making the distinction.

Is it necessary for the owner or captain of a ship to procure a license before he can purchase firearms to take on board his ship? It is sometimes necessary for the captain of a vessel to take firearms on board a ship in case of any trouble. Furthermore, it is customary to have on board a fishing vessel a swivel, or small cannon, to be discharged in a fog in order to let the fishermen when out in their boats, know in which direction to go to reach the vessel. Is it necessary for them to obtain a license in order to place this firearm on board the vessel?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no exception
for that class of persons, and therefore I think they would come under the law. I may point out that no respectable person will have any difficulty whatever in obtaining a permit. If the hon. gentleman will refer to the sections of the existing law which cover the granting of permits, he will find that the officers empowered to grant these permits are so numerous that certainly nobody at any port from which a vessel requiring to carry a firearm would have to leave will have the slightest difficulty in obtaining a permit.
By whom are the permits issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The list of officers
authorized to grant permits is numerous. It includes magistrates, mayors, officers of the Northwest Mounted Police and commissioners of police. The numeration was extended at the time the Act was passed so as to include every officer that within reason could be suggested as a person who might be entrusted with that authority, 'the view being to insure that in practically every part of the country every respectable person would have easy access to the officer authorized to grant the permit.
Is there any fee to be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
Is there a penalty in case of not obtaining a license?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, there is a penalty for a person having the arm without a permit, and there is a penalty for the man
who sells the arm if he does not satisfy himself that the party purchasing has a permit.
There must be a permit for every individual purchase?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
What about the question of jurisdiction on the high seas outside the three-mile limit?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to jurisdiction we
are not purporting to legislate in this Act to make it an offence to carry a firearm on the high seas outside the three-mile limit. What our power is in that regard would perhaps be a question connected with one of the resolutions on the Order Paper. At all events, power or no power, we are not pretending to exercise any such right by this legislation.

Do I understand that a
British subject [DOT]who is now the possessor of a shot gun may still keep it without obtaining a license?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
What about the child who owns an air rifle at the present moment, what becomes of him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether you could describe-

Are you afraid of his
Bolshevist activities?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would assume that
this law, like all other laws, would be applied with some degree of intelligence. I fancy that a child who might own an air gun would not be in very serious jeopardy if he did not obtain a permit. I want to be perfectly frank. The purpose is as I have explained, and we do not think it is imposing any hardship upon anybody, when we make it possible for any respectable person to .obtain a permit without any difficulty. The purpose is to enable us to obtain knowledge of the trafficking in dangerous firearms, and keep control over persons who have them in their possession. Police reports at different times have urged the great importance of this knowledge and control. In connection with applications for clemency it is astonishing how much crime is attributable to the ease with which people obtain firearms and the indiscriminate way they use them. We do think that the very slight inconvenience imposed upon respectable citizens is more than justified by the importance o,f our being able to control the possession of these dangerous weapons.

I do not see the logic in refusing a permit to the owner of a rifle and granting it to the owner of a shot gun. It seems 'to me that a shot gun at short range would do just as much damage as a rifle, probably more.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was pointed out that there is a much wider field of use for the shot gun for purposes entirely disconnected . with violence. If we are a trifle too severe on the man who owns a rifle-

But how many respectable citizens who go hunting every autumn have rifles at home? They will never think of applying for a permit, and they will be liable to great annoyance by some officious magistrate,-and his type is frequently met with in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This law, like every other law, will become known, and I do not think any respectable citizen will resent being called upon to take out a permit. On the contrary, I think all respectable citizens twill realize the importance of control in this matter, and will be glad to contribute to that control at the slight inconvenience Of applying for a permit. Of course, it is a most unfortunate thing, but law cannot be administered except upon the assumption-a very violent assumption I know-

That a man thinks.
Mr. DOHERTY -that men know and think.
Provided the law be reasonable; but this law does not seem to be reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have stated what seems to me to be reasonable.	^

But the men I have in mind have used rifles all their lives perhaps, and because the hon. minister and the Government for some reason or other have got it into their heads that Bolshevism or some other "ism" is rampant in the country they are going to force such men to run round for a permit. The most reasonable and law abiding citizens will not think of such a thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have a larger faith in the capacity for thought of the reasonable law-abiding citizens of this country.
But this is not a reasonable law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as I am capable of judging of what is reasonable and what is unreasonable, I think this is a reason-

able provision. Reasonable citizens who drive in automobiles-
The automobile is more dangerous than the rifle.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps it is. But automobile owners .are required to obtain licenses; and I might instance numerous other cases in which licenses are required. I think the hon. gentleman will find 'that his apprehensions will not be justified in the practical working out of this legislation. It cannot be reasonably suggested that because we have a law against the carrying of concealed weapons we are all liable at any moment to be stopped by a constable on the street and searched. How often does that happen to respectable citizens? On the other hand, this is a most invaluable safeguard in respect to citizens who do not happen to he reasonable or worthy to have in their possession arms of this kind.

My principal objection is that by this law a shot gun is excepted and a rifle is not. What distinction can be drawn between a shot gun and a rifle I do not know. Supposing I have a rifle in my possession at home, and before going away shooting I apply to some magistrate in the country for a permit; for some reason or other he refuses to issue me one; what becomes of my rifle? Do I give it to the magistrate? Do I throw it away? Or is any provision made for compensation for the confiscation of my property?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can only suggest that in that case the hon. gentleman should take the trouble of finding a reasonable magistrate,-and there are lots of them.

What meaning would the minis'ter attach to the word "shot gun" in the tenth line? A British subject is not required to obtain a permit to own a shot gun which he already posseesses. But in the list of things banned shot guns are not mentioned. I would think that "shot gun" was intended to cover all forms of guns and rifles.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The preceding Word
covers every kind of machine gun, rifle, gun, revolver, etc.
But not the shot gun?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It does not say "shot gun," but it covers every gun, and we make an exception for the shot gun already owned. "Shot gun" is already included among the weapons mentioned, and moreover would be included among "firearms,"

for it is a firearm. What was urged upon us as a reason for making this exception was* the very widespread extent to which farmers in this country, and particularly in certain sections, own shot guns and consider them as practically part of their equipment. It was thought that we should not make this law operative in respect to weapons of that kind already owned by them. The difference between the two situations is that in regard to* that particular kind of weapon the law is to apply only to those firearms which are hereafter acquired.

Why should this provision not read?- .
Provided that no British subject shall be required to obtain a permit with respect to any gun now owned by him.
What is the object of using the word "shot gun?"

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was thought that that expression would best cover the case of those persons who are already in possession of a weapon of this kind the principal purpose of which is for use in hunting. I do not say that the rifle is never used for hunting, but that is not its primary or principal purpose, as I understand it. On the other hand, it was reported to us that the shot gun is the weapon which the farmer keeps in his house and uses, more particularly in the western part of the country. The idea was to avoid withdrawing from a large class of the people a privilege which they had hitherto enjoyed. I can offer no fruther reason for the distinction. Perhaps it is not absolutely well founded, but there seemed to be good reason for making it. If experience should show that it is desirable to extend these requirements to other weapons, we shall be able subsequently to amend the law in that regard. In the meantime we have the general provision on the subject.
Will the permit be good all over Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no restriction upon the place where a permit issued by a competent officer may be used.

Does this clause apply to obsolete arms or arms that are used for purely decorative purposes? I know of several public places and dwellings where article*s enumerated here are used for decorative purposes only.
Panoplies.

Some of these
weapons are hundreds of years old; they
are collected by people who make a kind of hobby of that sort of thing. To require a permit for each arm of that kind would work considerable hardship. I do not know w'hat the permit costs; it may be free. But some of these articles might be difficult to name. We do not want to do injustice to a very large number of our citizens who are already in possession of many of these articles.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have to confess that I had not considered that possible event. I think it would be an extreme interpretation to say that a man* who had a gun such as is used for decorative purposes would be in possession of a firearm in the sense of this statute. If the hon. member thinks that the cases are so numerous and the probability of the law being interpreted to cover such cases so great as to necessitate an exception, I have no objection to making an exception to meet the case. I think, however, that we may safely count upon the word "firearm" being interpreted as being an arm susceptible of being used today as a firearm. We have had this sort of legislation for years, and I do not know that people who preserve, say daggers, as curios or mementos or objects of historical interest have ever been troubled under it. I think we may safely let the law stand in its present form, and if it gives rise to any cases of that kind we may take care of them. It is difficult to anticipate all the cases that might be conjured up as coming within the section,
Does the word "person" in this section include a corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The general Interpretation Act, and, I think, the interpretation clauses of the Criminal Code, make the word "person" include a corporation. I see no reason why a corporation should be entitled to have weapons of this sort with out permit any more than an individual person. Of course, possession on the part of a corporation must be possession on the part of some individual person; a corporation cannot act except through persons.

I think the minister is right in saying that the word "person" includes a corporation. I note that cannons are being distributed all around the country to corporations, who are accepting them as gifts from the Government. Will these corporations be obliged to go to a magistrate and get a license to hold those guns?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think they will; I do not see why they should not. I do not see why a corporation or a person should not

ibe required to get a permit to possess a cannon when we provide ample facility for the obtaining of a permit. Corporations as well as individual persons could help us out in that regard.

I would inform the minister that out West the rifle is just as common as the shot gun in the farmer's home. I look upon the shot gun as a more dangerous weapon than the rifle. I think both the rifle and the shot gun should,be allowed, as a concession to the farmers,
|Mir. DOHERTY: Of course, the hon. gentleman has a more intimate knowledge of western conditions than I have, but I tray say that from inquiry I made on the subject the impression that remained with me and with my colleagues-because we made inquiry on the subject that we thought was sufficient-was that the shot gun was the more usual and the more necessary weapon. It Is difficult for us, in passing a law of this kind, to begin differentiating between different classes of people. In the circumstances in which weapons of this sort are sources of danger, we do find that the rifle figures more frequently than the shot gun and that therefore there is a greater need for control of the possession of the rifle than there is for control of the possession of the shot gun. That is the result of our inquiry. The argument may get this far; that because we do feel that we ought to control the possession of the rifle, if hon. gentlemen persuade us that there is no distinction to be made between the rifle and the shot gun, we shall have to consider whether we ought not to withdraw the exception made in favour of the shot gun. I think that outside of weapons that can be concealed the rifle is perhaps the most important weapon for us to see, as far as we may, that it is only in the hands of proper people. I would sympathize with my hon. friend's objection if there was any real difficulty for any respectable man to get a permit, but, as I have said, we have provided to make it the easiest thing in the world for a respectable man to get a permit. At the time the statute went through the House, I accepted suggestions from everybody who could suggest to me an officer that might be authorized to give this permit, because I recognized, and I recognize still, that we ought not to make this a burdensome thing, and it is not a burdensome thing.
On section 3-signing pretended affidavit or declaration:

Wa.s it not the intention to limit this to improper use of an affidavit in the case only of judicial proceedings? There might be some tomfoolery about something that looked like a declaration that was not in a judicial proceeding at all. I would think that the intention of the Act was that if a person uses such a declaration or affidavit in any judicial proceedings he shall be subject to a penalty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The intention was to
make it an offence for any person to send a man out in possession of something that on its face is an affidavit sworn to before a proper officer, when it never was so sworn. There have been brought to my attention quite a number of instances where this has been done, and where, outside of actual judicial proceedings,, it has been used to perpetrate a fraud. For instance, it has been brought to my attention that in certain parts of the country there is a widespread practice among certain gentlemen authorized to issue marriage licenses, and who in the issue of the licenses, have to take affidavits from the person applying for the license, to leave with their clerk or lady stenographer the necessary form, and when any man came along and wanted a marriage license the lady would fill in the form with his name and so forth, and when our issuer of marriage licenses got back, without ever having seen the man, he certified at the bottom that that man had sworn to it. Now that is a serious offence. Any man who is authorized to administer oaths should certainly realize that he is not entitled to certify that a man swore to a certain thing when he did not swear to it.
The second paragraph deals with the offence of the man who puts the affidavit forward as being a proper affidavit. Many and many a transaction has been put through, quite outside the courts, upon the faith of an affidavit. It seems to me that the practice of going out and palming off these documents as affidavits which are really not affidavits calls for repression, and if we limit it exclusively to judicial proceedings we shall fail to reach a large number of oases that ought to be reached. I do not know why it should have happened, but there seems to have been a sort of outbreak of this thing. I have had communications from different sources calling my attention to the abuse made of these pretended affidavits, and as it happens these cases were not in judicial proceedings. In a judicial proceeding you have a judge and some authority to take pains to verify the affidavits.

But take the case with regard to marriage licenses. Certainly that is a very great abuse, if it prevails to any widespread extent, and in the particular cases which came to my knowledge, the gentleman who issued these licenses was surprised at the suggestion that he did wrong, and the young lady who had been employed in that particular instance was surprised to learn that she was doing anything wrong. She says " Why, for years I was in the employ of Mr. So-andsSo, and Mr. So-and-So, and Mr. So-and^So, all of whom were authorized to issue marriage licenses-"
Does the false affidavit affect the validity of the marriage?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, but the requiring of the affidavit is for the protection of the other consort, or any other people who may be interested. It certainly is a very grave evil, even if it should not go so far as to affect the validity of the marriage, that people should be enabled to avoid the consequences of perjury,-for if they did not swear to anything they cannot be convicted of perjury,- by making use of what purports to be an affidavit but which they know is not an affidavit. The purpose was not to confine the offence to judicial proceedings. If anybody gets into trouble, because he wants to get into trouble by sending out sham affidavits I do not think he is entitled to a great deal of sympathy, and if it be simply a joke, I have no doubt the magistrate will mete out the proper punishment. But it is a serious thing, and people ought to have it impressed on them that the oath is^ not a thing to be fooled with in reality or in appearance.
Referring for a moment to the section we have just passed, where there are several sons in a farmer's home will each member of the family who wishes to use the rifle have to have a separate permit?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Oh, no. The rifle is,
properly speaking, in the possession, I would take it, of the home. If the individual wants to take that rifle away in his own personal possession and use it, I think he would be required to have a permit, and that is for the purpose of keeping a check upon the people who use -these weapons. Any -one who wants to carry a firearm of that kind must ge-t a permit.

On section 7-betting, pool-selling and bookmiaking.
Does the minister become sponsor for this remarkable section? I do not profess to understand it myself but I take it that the minister knows all about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The section reproduces
the law as it stands, with all the existing restrictions upon the permissibility of organized betting. The reason it is so long and complicated is the fact that it repeats all the restrictions that already exist, and it adds certain further restrictions. In the first place, the organized betting is to be exclusively by the operation of the parimutuel machine; the bookmaker is gone. In the second place, the profit to be taken by the association or person conducting a race meeting is limited to the percentages mentioned in the section as follows:
Where the total amount staked or deposited on each race is under $20,000 . .	1%
$20,'00'0 but not exceeding $30,000..	..	6%
Over $30,0'00, but not exceeding $40,000.	5%
Over $40,000 but not exceeding $50,000..	4%
Over $-50,000	 3%
In addition the machines are to be subject to the approval of the officer of the Minister of Agriculture; the operation is to be carried on under his supervision. The machines are to be locked before the horses can be started, and if the proprietors of the race track do not devote what in the judgment of the Minister of Agriculture is a proper proportion of the moneys so derived from these percentages to giving prizes for the encouragement of horse breeding, the minister is empowered to require them to discontinue the use of the machine or in other words to prevent any organized betting on the race track. The purpose is to create a situation where no association will have the privilege of organized betting on its race track if the association is one that is in the business for what it can make out of it. It will prevent there being any big haul for the gentlemen who want to engage in this organized betting as a business,



and we expect that it will reduce the race tracks to those which are controlled by people who bona fide, carry on their racing for the sake of the sport and to whom the betting feature is purely incidental, something, which, according to the testimony laid before Mr. Rutherford the Commissioner, is, by a large number of people at all events, believed to be essential to keeping up a state of interest in the meetings and inducing people to support them. We think that the clause surrounds the privilege with every restriction with which it Can be surrounded if it is to be allowed to exist at all.

Is this machine that
the minister has spoken of capable of fraudulent manipulation? I do not know very much about these things but I have heard it said that some of the machines that are used, slot machines and that sort of instrument, can be so adjusted as to be made unfair to the man who is betting. I suppose the minister is satisfied that there is no such device in connection with the machine that is used on the race track?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have provided as
an additional precaution* that the machines used have to pass the inspection of an officer appointed by the Department of Agriculture for the purpose of seeing that there is no trick about them.
What is the object of making a distinction between trotting races and others?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The distinction is not
new; it exists in the present law and has existed in the past. Our information is that the great evils that are claimed to have resulted-and I think it cannot be questioned have resulted-from the abuse of the betting privilege have, whatever may be the occult reason, been more in connection with running races than wdth trotting races. I understand furthermore that trotting races very largely take place in connection with fairs, agricultural exhibitions and gatherings of that kind, and I am informed that the experience is that they do not generate the grave evils that have unfortunately surrounded the running race tracks. In regard to trotting races we are making no change in the law. Additional restrictions are being put on running races and I may say that a large number of restrictions had already been put on the running races which are not made applicable to trotting races.

How many race tracks are there in operation?
fMr. Doherty.]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not that information before me now, but they have grown considerably and that is one of the things that we hope this law will kill. We have reason to believe that quite a number of race tracks have sprung up as'money making things pure and simple, and it is in connection with these race tracks and moneymaking by persons running race tracks that we expect that the effect of this law will be to disinterest this class of people in racing associations, and that in the future we may hope to have racing controlled by people who are interested only for the sport and for the encouragement of the breeding of good horses and to whom the betting is a mere incident as the profit which they may get out of it is a mere incident.

On section 9-carnally knowing girl between 14 and 16:
What is the maximum punishment now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is to create a speci-fiv offence in regard to a girl between 14 and 16. As the law is at present it is an offence to have carnal knowledge of a girl under 14. There is no protection to a girl of 16. We are raising the age to 16 and making the punishment in the case of a girl between 14 and 16 not as severe as it is in the case of a girl under 14.
Consent is not material now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Consent under 14 is entirely immaterial. Consent under 16 will be immaterial in the future, but the punishment of a person committing an offence with a girl between 14 and 16 is not made as heavy as it is with regard to a girl under 14. In the case of a girl under 14 a man is liable to imprisonment for life and to be whipped. While we have extended the period of protection it has not seemed to Parliament in both instances in which it has dealt with it that the punishment should be as great in the case of this new offence as it was in the case of the old one.
What is the maximum punishment under the Code in the case of a girl between 14 and 16?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The present section, 301, reads as follows:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for life, and to be whipped, who carnally knows any girl under the age of fourteen years, not being his wife,

whether he believes her to be of or above that age or not.
So that if the girl is under the age of fourteen the man is liable to imprisonment for life. Where the girl is between fourteen and sixteen the man is liable to imprisonment for five years. There is a substantial difference between the penalties.

this section, but I would like to ask for an explanation from the minister in regard to subsection 2 dealing with the onus of proof. It is the easiest thing in the world for a man to lose his discharge papers, and unless he were given ample time to prove his identity he might suffer hardship.

On section H-Process not to issue for the arrest or summoning of a person outside a province without approval of Attorney General or a judge.
Will that not cause delay in having the process served. In Ontario the judges of the Supreme Court of the province all reside in the city of Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It may cause delay, but it is to be borne in mind that this i3 a clause applicable in the somewhat exceptional case where a warrant issued in one province is to be executed in another province. and the accused brought out of his 217J
province for trial. Now it has been urged that it is a very great hardship that it should be in the power of any irresponsible individual who goes and swears out a warrant to bring a man from Gaspe in the province of Quebec to, if you like, Vancouver, there to find that there is an unfounded charge against him. I may say that our attention was specially called to this in connection with prohibition legislation. The hardship of subjecting a man to be taken out of one province to be tried in another was very strongly urged, and this very objection made-that a man is liable to be brought out of his own province and nobody is responsible. This safeguard was adopted in that particular legislation, and it has been urged upon us that it would be desirable to make it of general application.
'Mr. PROULX:	In a province where
there are county court judges those judges could be added.

speechtext: I think there would be no objection to adding the words "or a county court judge."
It would be better to add the words, "or a county court."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then the section would read: "or a judge of the superior court or of a county court." I move that the section be so amended.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It will read as follows:
No warrant or -other process shall be issued in any province for the arrest or summoning of any person residing in another province without the approval of the Attorney General or a Judge of the Superior Court or of a County Court of the province where it is sought to issue the process.

speechtext:
I take it that the provision would not apply to the subpoenaing of a witness. The words are:
No warrant or other 'process shall be issued in any province for the arrest or summoning of any person residing in another province

The hon. gentleman of course knows that on a charge or complaint being laid against a man there issues a warrant for his arrest or a summons for him to appear, and I take it that the process in question is the process for the arrest of any person accused of an offence. I do not think the words cover the subpoening of a witness.

If the section was
amended to read, "no person shall be summoned or arrested upon a criminal charge," I think that would meet the objection I am taking. The Minister of Justice is aware that if I go before a magistrate and make an affidavit that I have reason to believe that a witness will not attend on an ordinary subpoena, I can get a warrant for his arrest. In a case of that kind a man would be arrested when merely wanted as a witness.

do with those laws; this is the Criminal Code.

On section 12-appeals in summary convictions in Saskatchewan and Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: (I move to amend this clause by inserting after the words "District Court" in line twenty-seven the words, "of the district in which the cause of the information or complaint arose." I may say that this amendment is being made at the request of the Attorneys General of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta in order to remove a doubt which existed under the present legislation as to what court an appeal should be taken to from a magistrate's decision. Under the present wording it has been argued that a convicted party was entitled to take his appeal to the nearest- district court, when that wasi the district court sitting at the place nearest to where he was convicted, without regard to whether it was within or without the judicial district. Both these law officers concur in the view that, it being desirable to avoid confusion, it should be made clear that the appeal must be to the district court in which the cause of action arose. As the present printed wording might still leave some doubt, I move that amendment.

Sometimes we have
confusion in our county of Cape Breton because we have two places at which the County Court sits, and it is rather doubtful which of those the appeal should be taken to. In civil and quasi-criminal matters the provincial law is that the appeal shall be to the court sitting at the nearest place to where the trial magistrate sat; but I do not think there is anything like that in the Criminal Code. There I think the rule is that the appeal shall be heard at the next sitting of the County Court, and that may not be nearest to the place where the magistrate tried the case. It seems to me it would be well to have it stated that the appeal be to the court sitting nearest to the place of the first trial. * Witnesses should not be taken away from home further than is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The provision now
seems to be for the province of New Brunswick precisely what we are trying to make it for the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. The provinces of Nova Beotia, New Brunswick and Manitoba are dealt with in subsection (c) of this section 749, and the provision is that the appeal shall be to the

County Court of the district or county where the cause of the information or complaint arose.

What I have in view
is this:	When the county court sits in
more than one place in the same district, under that law you have to go to the first sitting of the court whether it is the nearest court or not. Under our provincial law there is a provision that you may go to the court sitting at the place nearest to where the magistrate tried the case. In our county the court sits at Sydney, but it also sits twice a year, for the hearing of appeals and other matters, at North Sydney, on the other side of the water. If a case is tried at Sydney Mines or North Sydney the appeal must be heard, under the present law, at the first sitting of the court at Sydney, although that is not the nearest place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This particular provision does not impose any obligation with regard to the place at which the appeal shall be heard when the court sits at more than one place in the same district. Does this provision oblige the person appealing to go at the very next sitting? I ask that question for this reason:	In these matters
of procedure we have made it ,a practice not to modify provisions of that kind without consultation with the law officers of the province affected. Unless the hon. gentleman is absolutely clear that there is a substantial necessity for- modifying this provision I would rather not do so without consulting the law officers of the province.

I am not asking the
minister to do it on the spur of the moment. But there is a provision in the Criminal Code which says that if the magistrate's trial takes place more than fourteen days before the sitting of the higher court, then the person appealing must go to the first sitting of that court, regardless of whether or not it is the nearest or more remote from the place where the magistrate's trial was held. We find it inconvenient in our county because one court sits very much farther away from Sydney Mines than the one which sits at North Sydney. We are always careful that we do not give the notice of appeal to the wrong court. However, I do not ask the minister to change the provision now.

speechtext:
I shall take it up with
the Attorney General of the province with a view to further action.
