What special provision is this?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The proviso referred to, embodied in the statutes of 1919, was for the purpose of preventing an abuse that had grown up in different parts of the country with regard to cases where the accused had an option whether he should be tried by jury or take his trial before the magistrate or the judge of Sessions in different parts of the country. The abuse had grown up on the part of the accused, especially in Montreal and the province of Quebec, of making options for trial by jury upon being arraigned, and then, when the grand jury found, if it did find, a true bill against him, of withdrawing the option and declaring for trial before the Court of Sessions. The result was a very long delay between the arraignment of the accused and his trial, giving rise to many inconveniences,-the detaining of witnesses, and so on. Last year the law was amended doing away with the privilege, once the option had been made, of withdrawing that option and choosing to be tried before the magistrate or the judge of Sessions. It has been represented, however, that in the county of York the operation of that law has been such as unduly to encumber the Courts of Sessions and to cause other material difficulty in the administration of justice. It was thought proper to meet the request of the law officers of the province and except that particular county from the operation of this section.

As I understand it, the law previously provided that the accused could elect to be tried by a jury instead of by a judge and that he could later reverse that decision any say that he would prefer to be tried by the judge without a jury. The minister tells us that under the amendment of last year the prisoner could only elect once for all. Are we now going back to the old law so far as the county of York is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It will withdraw the county of York from the effect of the provision of last year's Act. Here is the proviso. It did not go as far as I suggested, but it limited the time within which a man might make his option. The proviso reads:
It an indictment has been preferred against a prisoner the consent of the prosecuting officer

shall be necessary to a re-election, and in such case the sheriff shall take no action on being informed of the prisoner's desire to re-elect unless such consent is given in writing.
This, I think, is the particular proviso:
And provided also that no prisoner shall have a right to re-elect later than thirty days before the day fixed for the next sittings of the court at which trials by jury can be had, unless the prisoner was committed for trial within forty days before the said date, in which event he must re-elect not later than ten days before the day fixed for the next sitting of the court at which trials by jury can be had.
The purpose was to prevent a man waiting until he gets to his court where he wa6 indicted, and finding out whether any true bill -would be found, and if there was a true bill found against him, withdrawing his option and re-electing. It is only the last proviso that is being made inapplicable. That is the one that was added last year. So the proviso that prevents a man within thirty days of the sitting of the court where he might be tried by jury altering his election will not in future apply to the county of York, and he will be entitled to alter his election up to the holding of the court. The proviso was made to facilitate the administration of justice, but it appears that in one particular district it did not operate to produce t-hat result. As I have said, in deference to this authoritative expression of opinion and the desire of the Attorney General and the law officers of the province, it did not seem to us there could be any objection to meeting their request.

I have no particular objection to limiting one's power to go before, a county court judge, because we are not by so doing depriving any one of his right 'to trial by jury, but I would hesitate to throw any obstacles in the way of a man's electing to be tried by jury at any stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This imposes no obstacles to his having trial by jury. What we are doing now is giving the prisoner greater liberty, because we are withdrawing the restriction which prevented his reelecting within thirty days of the coining on of the court. The prisoner in York has really a wider liberty than prisoners elsewhere.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 16-Attorney General of Quebec given power to apply for change of venue as well as accused when no criminal terms in district where accused is.
I do not know whether there are any Quebec lawyers here to-night, but in the province from which I come we are very strongly opposed to a change of venue in a criminal court case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I might explain ithe situation, which is perhaps a special one. I might say that this is being done at the request of the Attorney General of the province of Quebec. There provision is made for the holding of the term of the Court of King's Bench, criminal assizes, in each of the rural districts of the province, and it happens in numerous instances, because we are a very virtuous province, that when the time comes around in a district to hold a criminal term there is perhaps only one criminal, and that may be the case in three or four districts. Under the law as it stands, the Attorney General has no option hut to involve himself in all the expense of summoning juries, and all that goes with it, to hold a criminal term at the chief town of that district to try that one man. The same thing might happen in two or three other districts, where, if there was only one prisoner, each man would have a court unto himself. The Attorney General has represented, and I think the good sense of it must appeal to everybody, that under those circumstances he should have power to transfer these cases to some one district where the trial would he held, so that one court might dispose of a reasonable number of cases. It would relieve the province of very heavy expense to no purpose, and it would also relieve the prisoner from being exposed to being kept in gaol for a long time, waiting for his term in his own particular district, because naturally under these conditions terms are not held very frequently in such districts. On the one hand, it reduces the expense to the province, and on the other, it affords more speedy opportunity for trial of the accused, which to a man being held in gaol is a very important thing.

Does not the minister think it would be an economy to do away with jury trial in petty cases of theft for a few dollars? I understand that the accused often chooses trial by jury in order to gain time, and with a chance perhaps of seeing witnesses disappear or die and the evidence vanish, and then when the time comes to undergo trial before jury he chooses a trial before a magistrate. I think to do away with trial by jury in petty cases of this kind would save a great deal of money to the province and even to the Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
One would want to go
slowly in the face of such a proposal as to deprive a British subject of his right to trial by jury. I think, however, my hon. friend is mistaken in saying that people are entitled to trial by jury for thefts of very trifling sums. I do not know just what the amount is-
Ten dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. As to the abuse which the hon. member complains of, of a prisoner making option for a trial by jury to gain delay, and then withdrawing that option, by the provision of last year which I have just read, and which has been withdrawn from operation in the county of York-it remains in operation in the province of Quebec-the privilege of re-electing must be exercised at least forty days before the jury trials commence. So the prisoner is confined to a very short period within which he can exercise the privilege of re-election. If he has elected for trial by jury, he must in a limited time alter his choice, or adhere to his choice of trial by jury. I should be glad to consider, when we have lots of time to give to it, whether there ought to be further restrictions on trial by jury, but I should not like to decide hastily this evening to cut off a man's recourse to trial by jury.

I am glad to hear from the minister that the great province from which he comes is so free from crime of any kind, but I am shocked to recall the fact that yesterday-I think it was yesterday-he was very severely brought to task for arresting twro persons who were trying to escape a sentence of twenyt-five years for some extraordinary crime. I am rather disposed to think now that the men should have been left at large. It was a mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are among the
exceptions that prove the rule in our province.

There is another thing. Trivial criminal offences are always bailable, and the argument which the minister puts forward that offenders might be awaiting trial for a long time is of course answered by the fact that they can always get bail and be at large until a convenient time comes for trial. There is a provision in the code that if it is represented to a judge or the Attorney General that a man cannot obtain a fair trial in the county in which he has been arrested and is awaiting trial, if it is shown that there is danger
that either the Crown or the prisoner will not have a fair show, there can be a change of venue to be named by the judge with the advice of the Attorney General. The code also provides that the judge who changes the venue must provide for taking the witnesses of the defence to the more remote place, if it is far from the place in which he is arrested and it is more expensive to the prisoner to take his witnesses there. There must be provision for his expenses in getting his witnesses to that place. I do not notice anything in the law which the minister is putting into effect to-night to provide for a case of that kind. If a man is taken from the place where he should be tried to some other place he may not be able to pay for his witnesses, if he is a poor man; and if he is to be switched around, there must be provision for his witnesses' fees.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend will observe that the sections empowers the court to order a change of venue " in the manner hereinbefore provided," and the manner "hereinbefore provided" for changing the venue is that the order shall be made upon such conditions as to the payment of any additional expenses as the court or judge thinks proper to prescribe. So that in this case where it is decided "by competent authority " that a change is desirable, the accused will have the same protection which he has in, the case where the change of venue results from apprehension that there will not be a fair trail in -the district in which the accused is arrested,

of the acquaintances which he may have formed during his lifetime and the good effect he may have created in the community in which he has lived. For that- reason, I have always been strongly in favour of the principle of a man being tried in the place in which he has lived, where he is known, and where he is able to obtain the benefit of his reputation, whatever it may be. On the other hand, of course, he may have been a bad man and his reputation in the community might be against him. If. that is the case, it is only proper that he should be tried by men who are acquainted with his general reputation. I do not want to press the point further, but I cannot allow this Bill to pass without putting on record my view; I am dead against a change of venue in criminal cases unless it is absolutely necessary for two reasons, first, that the Crown cannot obtain a fair show, and second, that there is such a prejudice against the accused that justice will not likely be done to him.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 17-appeal to Supreme Court of Canada where judgment conflicts with the judgment of any other Court of Appeal :
What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It has happened that
the courts of Appeal of two provinces have pronounced, in each case unanimously, upon the same question arising under the criminal code, in absolutely diametrically contrary senses, and inasmuch as there is no appeal in criminal cases where the judgment of the Court of Appeal is unanimous -there is no appeal to the Supreme Court -there is no method of getting that jurisprudence settled. Now, the purpose of this section is to make it possible to get the jurisprudence settled, and I think the hon. member will realize that it is a highly undesirable condition, if we cannot find a remedy for it, where jurisprudence in courts applying one and the same law of Dominion-wide application, shall be left to differ in different provinces. I may say we have had representations from the judges of the different courts in the different provinces pointing out this anomalous condition of affairs. The remedy that is given provides that in such case hereafter the right of appeal is to the Supreme Court either on the part of the Attorney General or the accused, the purpose being to secure a determination which will settle the jurisprudence in the same sense for the whole of Canada in cases

where it happens that courts of final jurisdiction, as the law now stands come to different conclusions upon the same question and under the same law.
Does the clause refer to t'he Attorney General of the Dominion or of the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Attorney General of the province where the question arises.
There is nothing to indicate that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let me point it out.
Do not point it out; it is all right; let it go.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would point it out.
I am quite content if the hon. gentleman is satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It will only take a few moments. The parties to the suit are the Attorney General of the province on the one side and the accused on the other. I have no objection to adding a few words to make it clear, but I would understand it to be the Attorney General of the province because it is the Attorney General who is a party to the prosecution.
I do not ask that it be changed. I will be content with calling my hon. friend's attention to it.
Leave must be asked for in every case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, because the
Supreme 'Court must be satisfied that it is a case where there is a conflict.

I think that my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has raised a reasonable point. It means the Attorney General of the province but it should be made clear because we have nine provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have a saying in our province that "Many things go without saying, but they none the less go better when siaid." I beg to move that section 19 be amended by inserting after the words "Attorney General," in the 32nd line, the words "of the province."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
Would the minister say "of any other court of appeal." He means the court of appeal in any other province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes,
That is not stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As it happens, there is only one Court of Appeal in each province, and it is known as the Court of Appeal. I think the wording Should -stay as "it is. It does not necessarily mean that the court must be in another province, because if it happened that there were two Courts of Appeal in one province the appeal provided for in this clause could be taken.
Are there such?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know of any.

Unless they exist in
Quebec there are no provinces with two Courts of Appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then "any other Court of Appeal" must necessarily mean a Court of Appeal in some other province. It seems to me that it is better as it is.

I think it is better as
it is.
Bill reported and amendments concurred in.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When shall
the said Bill be read a third time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Now.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Does the
House give its unanimous consent that the Bill be now read a third time?
If it must have the consent of the House, I would say, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I offer my sincere and warm congratulations to the hon. gentleman upon the exercise of his great power.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Next sitting
of the House.
